title: Detroit Lions vs. Miami Dolphins preview, prediction: On Paper
summary: The Detroit Lions are beat up after a physical and emotional win over the Minnesota Vikings. And while they must travel to play a 1-6 Miami Dolphins team, they can’t afford to underestimate them. The NFC North is too competitive for a trap game, and the Dolphins are a little scrappier than they appear. But […]
full_text: MIAMI, FL - OCTOBER 21: Matthew Stafford #9 of the Detroit Lions in action against the Miami Dolphins at Hard Rock Stadium on October 21, 2018 in Miami, Florida. (Photo by Mark Brown/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions are beat up after a physical and emotional win over the Minnesota Vikings. And while they must travel to play a 1-6 Miami Dolphins team, they can’t afford to underestimate them. The NFC North is too competitive for a trap game, and the Dolphins are a little scrappier than they appear. But is there a real chance of an upset in Miami, or are the Lions clearly the better team? Let’s examine it in our Lions vs. Dolphins preview and prediction. It’s time for On Paper. Lions pass offense (8th in DVOA) vs. Dolphins pass defense (29th) The Lions’ passing offense remains one of their most reliable units on the team. While last week’s performance against the Vikings wasn’t explosive, it was certainly a lot better than most teams manage against Minnesota’s defense. While the DVOA ranking remains outside the top five, I still believe Detroit’s passing attack should be in that top tier. For the season, they rank: Fourth in passer rating (110.0) Seventh in yards per attempt (7.9) Third in dropback EPA (0.264) First in EPA/pass (+0.21) Fourth in dropback success rate (51.4%) Detroit is humming in all facets of their passing attack. In pass protection, the Lions allow the fifth-lowest pressure percentage (30.1%), rank seventh in pass-block win rate (54%), and rank third in PFF team pass-blocking grade (75.1). The Dolphins may have a worse pass defense than the Lions. Five out of the seven quarterbacks who have faced Miami have finished with a passer rating of 119.8 or higher. Granted, they’ve played some really good quarterbacks in Brock Purdy, Patrick Mahomes, Joe Burrow, and Drake Maye. Still, those quarterbacks have outperformed their year-long efficiency against Miami, and the DVOA ranking—which adjusts to opponents’ strength—proves this is a bad pass defense. Overall, they rank: 32nd in passer rating allowed (119.5) 32nd in yards per attempt (8.3) 32nd in dropback EPA (0.288) 32nd in dropback success rate (53.7%) This is the result of having an extremely young and inexperienced back seven. Though there is some recent hope for Miami’s pass rush. As Erik Schlitt pointed out in his Honolulu Blueprint , while the season-long stats don’t look great for the Dolphins’ ability to get to the passer (35.6% pressure rate, 18th; 4.2% sack rate, 28th), they’ve started to put things together. All nine of their sacks have come in the last four games, and they’ve posted a pressure rate of 39.5% or higher in three out of four of those games (league average is around 36%). Over those last four games, the Dolphins’ pass defense has been better, but certainly not good. From Weeks 4-8, Miami ranks 27th in dropback EPA (0.180) and 29th in success rate (50.7%). Player to watch: Sam LaPorta. It’s been a quiet few weeks for the Lions tight end, but Miami is allowing the sixth-highest yardage to tight ends (483 yards) and tied for the fourth-most touchdowns (six). Advantage: Lions +3. This is a top-five unit vs. a bottom-five unit. The only reason I’m not giving it a higher advantage is that some things are trending Miami’s way, and weather could also play a factor, with some slight chance of rain. Lions run offense (4th) vs. Dolphins run defense (26th) The Lions’ rushing attack still has frustrating bouts of inconsistency, but last week’s performance against the Vikings felt like a revelation. Whether Detroit’s sidecar formation was a Vikings-specific answer or the cracking of the code for the entire season, we’ll see. But it shows one thing for certain: Lions offensive coordinator Drew Petzing is capable of finding some answers. For the season, the Lions rushing attack now ranks: Ninth in yards per carry (4.6) 13th in rush EPA (-0.083) Third in success rate (47.0%) But I must continue to repeat myself that the negative plays are a big problem. The Lions’ 19.3% stuffed rate is sixth in the NFL. Those figures are down from last week (20.9%, third-highest), but it still remains an issue to track. Detroit’s power success rank also improved after last week, but they still rank just 24th, converting on just 59% of short-yardage situations. Still, it’s worth pointing out how both the offensive line and the running backs are doing their parts. Detroit’s line ranks third in adjusted line yards, eighth in run block win rate, and fourth in PFF run blocking grade. Meanwhile, Detroit’s backfield ranks sixth in rushing yards over expected per rush (+0.5), sixth in yards after contact per rush (3.38), and Jahmyr Gibbs ranks fourth in missed tackle forced rate (31.9%). This chart doesn’t exactly vibe with the Dolphins’ bottom-10 DVOA ranking. They’re not giving up a ton of yards nor a ton of yards per carry. So what gives? Let’s look deeper. Eighth in yards per carry allowed (3.8) 22nd in rush EPA (-0.078) 30th in rush success rate (43.9%) In short, it appears the Dolphins don’t give up a ton of big, explosive plays, but they essentially give up exactly what the offense needs. That’s backed by data. Miami has only given up 21 rushes of 10+ yards (t-14th), and just three rushes of 20+ yards (t-sixth fewest). The good news is the Dolphins are weak where the Lions’ run offense struggles. They’ve produced just a 14.9% stuffed rate (23rd), and they rank 21st in power success rate, allowing conversions on 68% of short-yardage situations. Player to watch: Jacob Rodriguez. The Dolphins rookie linebacker has been a fun player to watch thus far. Rodriguez has been credited with 30 “stops” per PFF (plays that are a failure for offense), which is second most among ALL NFL linebackers, not just rookies. Seventeen of those have come in the run, t-eighth most. Advantage: Lions +1.5 . I’m not sure I’d expect a huge game from Gibbs and company, given that Miami has not allowed over 150 rushing yards in a game. But Detroit should be fairly efficient on the ground. Dolphins pass offense (26th) vs. Lions pass defense (24th) It hasn’t been a great start to the year for Malik Willis in his new home, but it’s hard to blame him given the supporting cast. He’s got an extremely young receiving corps, a new offensive system, and an imbalanced offensive line. As a result, the Dolphins rank: 26th in passer rating (79.7) 20th in yards per attempt (6.9) 23rd in dropback EPA (0.014) 20th in dropback success rate (43.8%) The Dolphins aren’t a complete disaster, but they’re clearly below average. That said, there are some very interesting advanced statistics surrounding Willis. For one, he’s not afraid to chuck it deep. He currently owns the third-highest average depth of target (9.2), and his deep ball percentage of 16.4% ranks first in the NFL (yes, above Jordan Love, too). But he also ranks third in time to throw (3.05), suggesting he likely holds onto the ball too long—especially when you consider the Dolphins have the second-highest sack rate (10.3%). The offensive line is a mixed bag. Though they’ve allowed the second-highest pressure rate (43.2%), they rank 20th in pass block win rate and 31st in PFF pass blocking grade. The issue is that the left side of their offensive line is good-to-great (LT Patrick Paul is 14th in pass blocking grade, rookie LG Kadyn Proctor is improving) and the right side is a disaster (RT Austin Jackson is dead last in pass blocking grade, RG Jonah Savaiinaea is 63rd out of 76). And as mentioned before, the receiving corps is ridiculously young: Malik Washington is 25; Caleb Douglas is 23, and Chris Bell is 22. Young doesn’t mean bad, but it’ll take them some time to get adjusted to the NFL. Is the Lions’ pass defense actually getting better? It’s hard for me to tell. The raw numbers are improving, but as the chart above shows, they’ve also played some pretty bad passing offenses in the last few weeks. I’m not yet convinced. Overall, the Lions rank: 26th in passer rating…

title: NFL predictions: 4 keys to a Lions victory over the Dolphins in Week 9
summary: The Detroit Lions (5-2) and Miami Dolphins (1-6) will face off in Week 9 in a battle between two teams at different stages in their regime builds. The Lions have their eyes firmly set on the postseason and are riding a three-game win streak, while the Dolphins are in the early stages of a rebuild […]
full_text: Oct 30, 2022; Detroit, Michigan, USA; Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff (16) makes a pass against Miami Dolphins during the second half at Ford Field. Mandatory Credit: Junfu Han-USA TODAY Sports The Detroit Lions (5-2) and Miami Dolphins (1-6) will face off in Week 9 in a battle between two teams at different stages in their regime builds. The Lions have their eyes firmly set on the postseason and are riding a three-game win streak, while the Dolphins are in the early stages of a rebuild and are performing much like the Lions did in 2021 and 2022—lots of grit, but struggling to find success. “(Dolphins Head) Coach (Jeff) Hafley’s done a good job in his first year,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said on Wednesday. “A lot of similarities to—just reminds me a little of what we were when we came in. They’re young, they’re hungry, they’re active. They run, they hit, they hustle, they finish, try to play disciplined ball, and they’re playing that way.” This week’s prediction preview is sponsored by the folks at FanDuel Sportsbook , who currently have the Lions listed at +1600 to win this year’s Super Bowl and are currently 7-point favorites in Week 9 . Let’s take a closer look at this matchup and predict how the Lions will earn a victory over the Dolphins in this week’s Honolulu Blueprint. Dolphin s base scheme For a detailed look at the opposing scheme, check out our complementary breakdown piece: Lions Week 9 preview: Breaking down the Dolphins’ offensive and defensive schemes . Prediction 1: Lions slow down pass rush with runs up the middle Last Sunday, the Lions faced arguably the best defense in the NFL when they went head-to-head with the Vikings, and while the Dolphins are on the opposite end of the rankings spectrum, some of the strategies the Lions used against Minnesota will transfer over to this week’s game against Miami. The Dolphins defense enters this game 29th in DVOA, 24th in points allowed (25.9), 24th in yards allowed per play (5.7 ypp), and are dead last in the NFL in three areas: EPA per play (+0.10), EPA per pass allowed (+0.26), and passing yards allowed per play (8.3). However, this defense is showing growth in pressure rate. Looking at season totals, the Dolphins’ pressure numbers could be a bit deceiving: 31st in total pressures (77), 18th in pressure rate (35.6%), 30th in total sacks (9), and 28th in sack rate (4.2%). But when you look at the splits from their last four games, you can see the improvement: at Vikings: 17 pressures, 39.5% pressure rate, 4 sacks, 9.3% sack rate vs. Bengals: 11 pressures, 33.3% pressure rate, 0 sacks, 0% sack rate at Jets: 15 pressures, 45.5% pressure rate, 2 sacks, 6.1% sack rate vs. Patriots: 13 pressures, 48.1% pressure rate, 3 sacks, 11.1% sack rate If we isolate the games against the Vikings, Jets, and Patriots, we see nearly 60% of the defensive pressures and 100% of the Dolphins sacks. When you look at how the Dolphins have generated pressures and sacks, most of those situations come from stunting their defensive linemen. Last week against the Patriots, the Dolphins sacked the quarterback once on an end-of-half situation, with the other two sacks coming off a stunt where an edge rusher loops behind the interior defensive lineman and twists inside. We also saw stunts get home against the Vikings in Week 4. To counter the Dolphins’ stunts, offenses have been attacking the middle of the defensive line with their rushing attacks; teams are running inside 53% of the time, the sixth-highest rate in the NFL. While the Lions have preferred to lean on their outside-zone rushing scheme, we saw last week against the Vikings that Detroit has a formula to get downhill on inside runs. Now, the Lions don’t necessarily need to deploy a full-house set (three players in the backfield) again, but it would certainly be effective against the Dolphins’ Wide-9 base 4-3 defense. Prediction 2: Lions cross the zone to open the field for Goff While all defenses are complex, at their core, the Dolphins split their defensive personnel almost evenly between a base 4-3 (three linebackers) front and a “Big Nickel” (three safeties) formation. Regardless of set, they spend about 80% of the time in zone coverage, with half of that time spent between single-high (Cover-1, -3) and two-high (Cover-2, -4, -6) safety sets. When they deploy man coverage, they run exclusively single-high Cover-1. Depending on the safety formation, Lions quarterback Jared Goff will have to find the holes in the zone to exploit, but those gaps can widen if the Lions stretch the Dolphins laterally with their passing game. Based on the games I watched, the Dolphins’ defenders settle in their zones and tend to be slow to react to crossing routes in front of them. When offenses find success on crossers and stretch the zones across the field, that opens gaps down the deep seams, where speed receivers—hey, Jameson Williams—have found chunk plays. If the Lions can slow the Dolphins’ pass rush with run up the middle, then stretch the secondary laterally, they’ll have an opportunity to chew up yards in a variety of ways. Prediction 3: Lions match physicality; prevent explosive runs When the Dolphins lost their dynamic running back De’Von Achane to an ACL injury in Week 3, many thought Miami’s rushing attack would struggle. However, second-year back Ollie Gordon has stepped into a starting role, and the Dolphins’ new downhill, physical rushing attack has proved to be an asset, even outproducing their early-season statistics, save last week vs. the Patriots. With quarterback Malik Willis adding another element to the run game through RPOs and scrambles, stopping the run will likely be the Lions’ top priority. On paper, their raw numbers look good: rushing for 123.3 yards per game (11th), averaging 4.4 yards per carry (11th), -0.03 EPA per rush (10th), 26 runs that gain 10+ yards (7th), and explosive runs 16.7% (3rd). However, there are some concerning numbers that point to struggles with consistency, including: Rushing DVOA: 26th Rushing success rate: 38.7% (20th) Stuffed rate: 20% (26th) Adjusted line yards: 3.64 (27th) The Dolphins will want to establish their rushing attack against the Lions, and Detroit will need to match that downhill physicality. It wouldn’t be surprising to see the Lions spend a lot of time in base early as both teams work to control the trenches. Expect seven and eight defenders in the box pre-snap, and a situational spy to track Willis is likely. With changes coming to the Lions’ linebacker roles, Detroit will need Derrick Barnes, Trevor Nowaske, and Malcolm Rodriguez to elevate their games and keep the explosive runs in check. Prediction 4: Lions pass rushers get after Willis If the Dolphins can establish the run, they do a nice job of running play-action behind it and finding success. But that’s not always an option for Miami’s offense, and the inconsistencies in the run game have forced Willis to create opportunities on his own. Willis is talented—we saw that in Green Bay—comfortable passing from the pocket, and able to extend plays by escaping outside. But with limited support, he holds onto the ball too long, takes sacks, or misses his targets because his accuracy gets loose/inconsistent on the run. Miami’s offensive line is average at best (see below) and doesn’t hold up well against pressure, and while the Dolphins receivers have unique skills, they lack a true playmaker and currently rely on two rookies—Caleb Douglas and Chris Bell—in starting wide receiver roles. As a result, Miami’s passing offense numbers are near the bottom of the league: Pass yards per game: 166.7 (30th) Pass yards per play: 6.9 (20th) EPA per pass: -0.16 (24th) Explosive passes: 24th Willis EPA per dropback: -0.10 (27th) Willis EPA per pressure: -0.70 (36th) Pressures rate allowed: 43.2% (31st) Sack rate allowed: 10.3% (31st) The Lions would benefit by giving Willis no relief. Entering this game, the Lions have registered 116 pressures (5th best), a 35.8%…

title: 8 Detroit Lions coordinators takeaways: Kelvin Sheppard gets emotional
summary: On Thursday, all three Detroit Lions coordinators spoke with the media. The three sessions were highlighted by defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard talking emotionally and passionately about Jack Campbell, and the team’s response to his serious injury. Here are my eight takeaways from the entire day of press conferences. Offensive coordinator Drew Petzing Where do these […]
full_text: Detroit Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard watches warmup ahead of the game between Detroit Lions and Minnesota Vikings at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co On Thursday, all three Detroit Lions coordinators spoke with the media. The three sessions were highlighted by defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard talking emotionally and passionately about Jack Campbell, and the team’s response to his serious injury. Here are my eight takeaways from the entire day of press conferences. Offensive coordinator Drew Petzing Where do these unique ideas come from? The Lions pulled out a couple of new tricks last week against the Vikings: a “sidecar” formation with two tight ends hugged to one side of the backfield, and a semi-trick play involving Amon-Ra St. Brown lined up 15 yards off the line of scrimmage to get a running start before catching the ball. Both adjustments were extremely successful for Detroit, so Petzing was asked where he found inspiration for them. When it comes to the tight end formations that helped out the run game, Petzing said they take ideas from everyone, but singled out run game coordinator/offensive line coach Hank Fraley. “A lot of the run game starts with Hank,” Petzing said. “And I think he does a great job of putting that stuff together and staying creative and making it hard to defend, but also doing things that are comfortable to us that we can go out and execute at a high level.” As for the St. Brown play, that has been credited to pass game coordinator Mike Kafka. While the exact origin of that play isn’t clear, Petzing thinks Kafka’s connections to Northwestern—where Chip Kelly is doing some unique things—may have played a hand. “He’s a Northwestern grad and Chip Kelly’s over there doing some pretty innovative stuff right now. So, I’m sure some of it came from there,” Petzing said. He also admits there’s been some CFL influence lately. “The CFL, I’ve seen some CFL tape over the last two months, but you’re always looking for just different ways to be hard to defend,” Petzing said. Believing in 12, 13 personnel Through the first seven games of the season, the Lions were not running the ball well with more tight ends on the field. Exhibit A: You're definitely onto something. Lions' EPA/rush by formation: 11 personnel: 0.06 (10th) 12 personnel: -0.07 (17th) 13 personnel: -0.48 (28th) (via @SumerSports ) https://t.co/rUOeIW00VF — Jeremy Reisman (@DetroitOnLion) October 29, 2026 But Detroit was fantastic with 12 (one running back, two tight ends) and 13 personnel against the Vikings. So I asked Petzing why he chose to stick with it. The answer is that it was sometimes not about the personnel, but either execution or finding the right matchups for each week. “Some of those metrics to me are, ‘Was it scheme? Was it execution? We lost somewhere that didn’t have anything to do with the personnel we had on the field,’” Petzing said. “So, I generally think of it much less from that standpoint and much more from a, ‘Can we dictate a defense? Can I move gaps around? How do they want to play those personnels?’ It probably has a lot more to do with what they’ve put on tape against certain areas than necessarily how we’ve been against teams that aren’t them, if that makes sense.” Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard Finding strength through his own players When Jack Campbell went down in the fourth quarter of Sunday’s game, Sheppard admitted he couldn’t hold back the tears. As he fought through his own emotions, he found strength looking at the players around him. While they, too, were obviously emotional, he was inspired by how players like Aidan Hutchinson were using the moment as a rallying cry. “As I looked at players crying on the field, keeping my emotions intact, I’ll be lying to say I wasn’t crying. And where I was able to find my strength was my players,” Sheppard said. “And seeing tears roll down Aidan Hutchinson’s eyes and hearing them say, ‘We’re about to do this for 46.’ And once we have got to the sideline, I know you guys saw the moment of unity was prayer. Because in that time, I believe there’s times in life where you can lean on people. You can lean on people that are strong.” Then, on the first play back from the break—a critical defensive fourth down—Sheppard did something he rarely does: blitz on fourth down. Why? He saw the passion in his players. “We’ve never pressured on fourth down. And I know I’ve gotten asked why, what call, why that call in that moment? And it’s because when I looked at our players, I looked at that call sheet and I said, ‘Let’s go for 46.’ I heard Aidan and I said, ‘Let’s do it,’” Sheppard said. Sheppard called the performance from Hutchinson and Derrick Barnes on that play “remarkable,” as they pressured Kyler Murray into a rushed, incomplete pass. Awesome Jack Campbell story To put that previous story in context, Sheppard explained just how much Campbell means to him. He brought up a moment from earlier this year. After the first four games of the season, there was a lot of outside noise about Sheppard and his job security. As the team prepared for the Arizona Cardinals, Campbell visited Sheppard in his home, and promised he would play his heart out for him. “When the heat was on me, that’s why I spoke the way I did—because of what my players were telling me. You guys have no idea. Jack (was) sitting on my couch before the Arizona week telling me he’s going to play for me. I’ll leave it at that,” Sheppard said. Putting football aside Sheppard said that the messaging on Wednesday for the team was to put football aside first before they can transition to game-planning. That goes back to one of his main tenants of coaching football. “You better understand the person before the player or you’ll never get to the player, ever,” Sheppard said. “You’ll never know how to talk to him. You’ll never know how to make him go. You’ll never understand why he’s doing things. You’ll never understand why he’s playing football if you don’t know that stuff. So, I always start there. I always have. I’ve always believed in that.” Sheppard also credited Dan Campbell with starting the week by immediately putting to the football to the side and allowing players a platform to talk through things. “When he starts the team meeting, football’s over there right now. Let’s talk about it. ‘Does anybody want to stand up and talk? Does anybody?’ And allowing that platform, allowing the vulnerability of people, everybody sees this game as a macho game. Real, real strength, real leadership is being vulnerable, understanding your weaknesses, understanding you don’t have it all figured out and knowing where to lean on people. And that’s what we’ve done as a team. That’s what we’ve done as an organization. And it’s the reason why we all enjoy being here.” The linebackers that remain With the Campbell and Jimmy Rolder injuries, focus turns back to the likes of Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez, Trevor Nowaske, and Joe Bachie to step up. These players have been around the defense for several years now, and Sheppard knows them well and trusts them. “I raised these other guys that’s about to play. Malcolm Rodriguez and Derrick Barnes. Those are my little brothers and they know the standard,” Sheppard said. “They both have worn the green dot before. So, this isn’t like a first time ordeal for either one of them because that load might get shared. We’re still working through that, but I’m confident in either one of them. And even a guy like Bachie, who everybody in this room is like, ‘Bachie, Bachie’, he’s number 35. He’s going to have a role in this game and we trust him wholeheartedly if he needs to put on the green dot to stand in front of that unit.” Special teams coordinator Dave Fipp Jake Bates’ miss wasn’t really his fault Fipp revealed that Jake Bates’ missed 40-yard field goal—his first missed kick of the season—wasn’t really his fault. Holder Jack Fox’s non-holding hand was…

title: Before the Roar: Previewing Detroit Lions vs. Miami Dolphins
summary: Just like that, we are already in Week 9 of the 2026 NFL season, where the 5-2 Detroit Lions will make their way down to South Beach for a matchup with the Miami Dolphins. To break everything down ahead of the inter-conference tilt, my good friend Meko Scott and I are back with a new […]
full_text: Just like that, we are already in Week 9 of the 2026 NFL season, where the 5-2 Detroit Lions will make their way down to South Beach for a matchup with the Miami Dolphins. To break everything down ahead of the inter-conference tilt, my good friend Meko Scott and I are back with a new episode of “ Before the Roar. ” Coming off of what a big and emotionally taxing win over the Minnesota Vikings in Week 8, the Lions are hoping to extend their winning streak to four games against a Dolphins team that is still trying to find their way under first-year coach Jeff Hafley. Despite only having one win on the season, Miami has been competitive in more games than you would think—especially considering the amount of salary cap dollars being paid to players who are no longer with the franchise. Offensively, things center around the running game in Miami. Quarterback Malik Willis is averaging over six yards per carry, and running back Ollie Gordon is a powerful, efficient runner in offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik’s offense. Can the Lions’ run defense continue to stack solid performances against a team that will no doubt be looking to keep the ball out of the Lions’ hands as much as possible? On the defensive side of the ball, the Dolphins have some really nice standout players including second-year defensive end Chop Robinson, and rookie linebacker Jacob Rodriguez. However, they are certainly having some struggles in the secondary, which could end up being an issue against the Lions’ high-flying passing attack. You can watch the entire episode right here , as well as listen wherever you get your podcasts. title: Lions, Vikings mic’d up video shows redemption arc for Jameson Williams
summary: After a win, the Detroit Lions always release their own version of a “mic’d up” compilation from the game. Their “Sights and Sounds” videos are always worth your time, as they incorporate unique camera angles along with Dan Miller radio calls and mic’d up moments that you can’t get anywhere else. This week’s episode detailing […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 01: Detroit Lions wide receiver Jameson Williams (1) catches a pass in the corner of the end zone for a game-winning touchdown during the fourth quarter of a regular season NFL football game between the Minnesota Vikings and the Detroit Lions on November 1, 2026 at Ford Field in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Scott W. Grau/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images After a win, the Detroit Lions always release their own version of a “mic’d up” compilation from the game. Their “Sights and Sounds” videos are always worth your time, as they incorporate unique camera angles along with Dan Miller radio calls and mic’d up moments that you can’t get anywhere else. This week’s episode detailing the Detroit Lions’ 19-15 win over the Minnesota Vikings is can’t-miss. Obviously, it was an emotional game with Jack Campbell’s traumatic injury, and I think One Pride Productions does a good job covering that moment with grace and compassion while properly conveying the gravity and emotions of the moment. One other aspect of the game they uncovered was a moment of redemption that may have gone overlooked. This week, Lions receiver Jameson Williams was mic’d up, and it captured a couple of very interesting moments. Williams was involved in two extremely critical plays in the game. The first was his biggest mistake of the afternoon. It was the fourth quarter, and the Lions led 12-7. They had just gotten an emotional fourth-down stop on defense, and it was up to the offense to extend their lead and bleed some of the remaining 13 minutes of game time. Facing a third-and-inches, Jared Goff ran a QB sneak up the middle for a first down. But Williams had not properly reported as off the line of scrimmage, causing the refs to call illegal formation. Detroit would not convert the third-and-6, and they punted it back to Minnesota. As he was coming off the field, dejected, Williams was met with a coaching staff that had a message for him: “You owe us,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said. “I know, I know, I know,” Williams replied. The Vikings capitalized on Williams’ mistake, driving the length of the field to take the lead 15-12 with just under nine minutes remaining. That’s when Lions receivers coach Scottie Montgomery repeated the message to Williams. “You owe us,” Montgomery said. “Go back, make a play. I know the frustration. It [redacted] sucks. But we know you’re in. So stay in, okay?” “Yup,” Williams replied. What ensued was one of the Lions’ most impressive drives of the season. Detroit went 69 yards on just seven plays, led by five rushes for 57 yards—all of at least 9 yards. The cameras show Williams blocking is ass off the entire time. And on the first snap of Detroit’s goal-line offense, Jared Goff pulled the rug out from underneath the Vikings defense with a play-action pass to a wide-open Williams. As he sprinted toward the sideline following his game-winning catch, Williams reminded the staff of his redemption. Campbell: “Way to pay us back! That’s what I’m talking about!” Williams: “Hey! I owe you, don’t I? I owe you, don’t I?” Then, to Montgomery: Williams: “Hey! I owe you, don’t I? Montgomery: “Let’s go!” Williams: “I still owe you! I still owe you! Aw, yeah! Aw, yeah!” It’s a great moment caught on tape by the One Pride Production crew. You can watch the entire video below:

Mandatory Credit: Sam Navarro-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Detroit Lions (5-2) and Miami Dolphins (1-6) will square off in Week 9, with the Lions looking to extend their three-game winning streak—and the Dolphins seeking their second win of the season. “(Dolphins Head) Coach (Jeff) Hafley’s done a good job in his first year,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said on Wednesday. “A lot of similarities to—just reminds me a little of what we were when we came in. They’re young, they’re hungry, they’re active. Pressure rate: 43.2% (31st); Time to pressure: 2.77 (27th) Sacks allowed: 21 (21st); Sack rate: 10.3% (31st) RPO/rollout/bootleg concepts with QB Malik Willis to buy time in muddy pocket Dan Campbell on Dolphins offense: “Offensively, they really have an athletic offensive line that’s got mass. They run a versatile scheme. (RB Ollie) Gordon is a heavy back. You give him a lane, and he can hit it, hit it with speed, build the speed, and that’s where he gets dangerous. You let him hit the line of scrimmage with any type of speed and any crease and he can go. […] There’s a ton of this eye candy and motions and cutting the defense off. title: NFL trade deadline rumors: Lions, Bears could compete for same players
summary: The NFL trade deadline is coming soon (next Tuesday), and with such a tightly contested NFC North, there could be an arms race on the horizon. Currently the Minnesota Vikings lead the division at 6-1, but the 5-2 Detroit Lions and 6-2 Chicago Bears are close behind, and both teams are hunting to add more […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 14: Head coach Ben Johnson of the Chicago Bears and Head coach Dan Campbell of the Detroit Lions shake hands following the game at Ford Field on September 14, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The NFL trade deadline is coming soon (next Tuesday), and with such a tightly contested NFC North, there could be an arms race on the horizon. Currently the Minnesota Vikings lead the division at 6-1, but the 5-2 Detroit Lions and 6-2 Chicago Bears are close behind, and both teams are hunting to add more talent before Tuesday’s deadline. In fact, according to ESPN insider Dan Graziano, both the Lions and Bears could be hunting for the same players. In one of his latest pieces for ESPN, Graziano said both the Lions and Bears have made calls about acquiring a cornerback. “The Bears made their big move for [Jeffery] Simmons, but they’re still poking around on potentially available cornerbacks, as are the Lions,” Graziano wrote this week. “Detroit might also be in the market for help at linebacker, particularly in the wake of the terrible injury to mainstay Jack Campbell.” It’s no surprise to hear that the Lions are still searching for a cornerback. The team admitted they were in the market for Joey Porter Jr. before he was eventually traded to the Dallas Cowboys. And the Lions’ cornerback situation hasn’t really changed since. While D.J. Reed is certainly playing better as the team’s No. 1 cornerback in recent weeks, Detroit is still seeking a No. 2 cornerback while rotating through the likes of Roger McCreary, Rock Ya-Sin, Khalil Dorsey, and Ennis Rakestraw. The Bears, who already made a big trade deadline move by sending two first-round picks and more to the Titans for defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons, have also dealt with some issues in the secondary. No. 1 cornerback Jaylon Johnson is currently ranked 103rd out of 106 qualifying cornerbacks in PFF coverage grade (32.1), while CB2 Malik Muhammad isn’t faring much better (52.5, 78th). At this point, it isn’t clear which cornerbacks are available to acquire at the trade deadline. But some of the more commonly thrown around names are Eagles cornerback Riq Woolen, Commanders cornerback Mike Sainristil, Dolphins cornerback JuJu Brent, and Chargers cornerback Donte Jackson. A month ago, we also compiled a list of defensive backs that the Lions could target at the trade deadline . We’ll see if either team can pull off a move with just days remaining before the deadline.

title: Discussion: Which Detroit Lions player needs to step up most in light of injuries?
summary: The Detroit Lions’ Wednesday injury report was as long as it’s been all season. On top of Jimmy Rolder being placed on injured reserve earlier this week, the following Lions players were estimated to not be able to practice: Additionally, these players were estimated to be limited in practice: That’s six Lions defenders and nine […]
full_text: Aug 3, 2026; Allen Park, MI, USA; Detroit Lions linebacker Malcolm Rodriguez (44) smiles as he talks with linebacker Derrick Barnes (55) following Detroit Lions training camp. Mandatory Credit: Paul Barnick-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Detroit Lions’ Wednesday injury report was as long as it’s been all season. On top of Jimmy Rolder being placed on injured reserve earlier this week , the following Lions players were estimated to not be able to practice: C Cade Mays (ankle) EDGE DJ Wonnum (concussion) LB Jack Campbell (neck) CB D.J. Reed (hip) Additionally, these players were estimated to be limited in practice: RB Jacob Saylors (neck) WR Amon-Ra St. Brown (rib) LB Amen Ogbongbemiga (toe) S Kerby Joseph (knee) S Brian Branch (concussion) That’s six Lions defenders and nine total players with their status up in the air this week. It’s far too early to declare any of these players definitively out this week (outside of Kerby Joseph— Dan Campbell already said he won’t play this week —and Jack Campbell), but there’s a pretty good likelihood the Lions will be missing at least a couple of these players. So today’s Question of the Day is: Which Lions players need to step up the most vs. the Dolphins? My answer: It feels like the answer has to come on defense. With Campbell and Rolder out, there will certainly be a ton of extra pressure on the linebacker room. Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez, and Trevor Nowaske are the most likely starters for Detroit this week, and we’ve seen a lot of ups and downs from this group. The good news is that they all have plenty of experience on defense. The bad news is that none of them bring the consistent play-making ability of Campbell, nor the leadership of Detroit’s defensive captain. But relief can also come from a different position. Covering the middle of the field has been a challenge, and it’s not necessarily a strength of the current linebacking corps. This would be a huge week for the safeties to step up. While it’s unclear if Branch will be available this week, I’m really looking for Chuck Clark and Keith Abney to elevate their games. Abney has been up and down, as you’d expect from a rookie who made a midseason shift from cornerback to safety. But I’ve been pretty disappointed with how Clark has played. He was supposed to bring communication and discipline to the position, but mental errors have plagued the back end (admittedly, not all his fault). Malik Willis is not afraid to throw deep or utilize the middle of the field, so I’d love to see a clean game from the safeties to help out the ailing linebacker position. title: Packers Injury Report: Keisean Nixon, MarShawn Lloyd downgraded on Thursday
summary: The Green Bay Packers held a padded practice inside the Don Hutson Center today, where they were a little more banged up than initially thought. After being a full participant on Wednesday with no injury status, running back MarShawn Lloyd appeared on the injury report on Thursday with a knee and was given “limited participant” […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers held a padded practice inside the Don Hutson Center today, where they were a little more banged up than initially thought. After being a full participant on Wednesday with no injury status, running back MarShawn Lloyd appeared on the injury report on Thursday with a knee and was given “limited participant” status. For what it’s worth, players who drop out of practice with an injury are also given that status, so that’s possibly what happened to Lloyd. The Packers’ running back numbers are good right now, as they’re already healthy scratching Kaleb Johnson when the whole unit is healthy, so it’s unlikely that Green Bay will need to make a roster move if Lloyd can’t play against the New England Patriots on Sunday. The other bad news out of today is that cornerback Keisean Nixon, who was a game-time decision with a groin injury last week, dropped from being a limited participant on Wednesday to a non-participant on Thursday. If he can’t go, it’s likely that he’d be replaced by Carrington Valentine, who stepped in for Brandon Cisse the last time that outside cornerback reps were made available. Keep an eye on that situation tomorrow, when the Packers will make their first game statuses of the week. Other non-participants in practice today, beyond Nixon, were tight end Josh Whyle (concussion), center Sean Rhyan (ankle), offensive lineman Travis Glover (knee) and linebacker Zaire Franklin (shin). Rhyan won’t be going on the injured reserve, head coach Matt LaFleur clarified in the pre-practice press conference. The limited participants for Green Bay on Thursday, aside from Lloyd, were running back Chris Brooks (ankle-IR window opened), receiver Christian Watson (rib), left guard Aaron Banks (knee) and edge defender Micah Parsons (knee-PUP window opened). The Patriots got their own share of bad news today when slot defender Marcus Jones was added to the injury report with a foot injury and was a non-participant in practice. The other non-participants for them today were running back TreVeyon Henderson (illness), receiver A.J. brown (ankle/knee) and tight end Hunter Henry (foot). title: Drake Maye vs. Jordan Love: Which is the better quarterback?
summary: We here at Acme Packing Company are careful not to judge quarterbacks on raw counting statistics unless they suit our needs. For instance, we love Brett Favre’s longevity stats, yards, and touchdowns, but when it comes to interceptions, for all QBs with at least 2500 attempts, he’s 75th (out of 147). Not too shabby! But […]
full_text: (Photo by Megan Briggs/Getty Images) | Getty Images We here at Acme Packing Company are careful not to judge quarterbacks on raw counting statistics unless they suit our needs. For instance, we love Brett Favre’s longevity stats, yards, and touchdowns, but when it comes to interceptions, for all QBs with at least 2500 attempts, he’s 75 th (out of 147) . Not too shabby! But usually, especially lately, counting stats have worked against us because the Packers run at SUCH a slow pace that Jordan Love really can’t rack up any significant yardage or touchdown totals. And so, typically we rely on things like EPA (Expected Points Added) and CPOE (Completion Percentage Over Expected), which makes us feel all warm and fuzzy. But fast forward to THIS season and suddenly Jordan Love LEADS THE LEAGUE IN PASSING YARDS . And also attempts, which is not as good, but still noteworthy. This is also new and fascinating, because we’ve all been asking to let Jordan cook for quite a while, but with all that volume, plus a trash running game (and some other factors, which we will get to), he hasn’t really been himself from an efficiency standpoint. He’s still more efficient than an average quarterback with .15 EPA per play (down significantly from .289 last year), and so the offense still works, but it’s a big drop. On that point, the only quarterback who had a better EPA per play last season was this week’s opponent, Drake Maye (.322). Maye is in his third season, and unquestionably great, but just how great is still a bit of a mystery. Last year he was probably the best quarterback in football, leading the way in EPA per play and the NextGenStats’ version of CPOE, which is widely regarded as the most accurate version. But like Love, Maye didn’t pass that much, finishing 12th in attempts with 492 (Love was 19th with 439, but he also missed two games. They were very close on a per-game basis). Maye’s numbers are still good this year as he’s third among active starters in EPA per play (.279, down almost .05 from last year), but his volume has ALSO fallen as he ranks 17 th in pass attempts behind players like Geno Smith and CJ Stroud. His CPOE has also decreased by over 50%, and he ranks seventh instead of first. Maye is, I think, having an objectively better season than Love in all the ways that matter from an individual player perspective. However, Love has almost certainly been the more valuable player, because when you are adding value to a football team, volume absolutely matters. One of the big reasons the Patriots have thrown fewer passes than the Packers is because (how best to put this), the Patriots’ running game doesn’t suck as much as Green Bay’s . None of this is hyperbole, and it’s important to understand that both running games do in fact suck. The Pats as a unit have run 240 times for a 4.1 YPC average, however, that average is dragged up by Drake Maye scrambles. The top two Patriots running backs, TreVeyon Henderson and Rhamondre Stephenson, both average under four yards per carry, and have combined for 148 carries. The Packers as a unit average a ridiculously terrible 2.9 yards per carry, and as a result, they’ve only run the ball 170 times. The Patriots are definitely better, and they have definitely been better running AND passing without question. Their offense, by any account, should be MUCH more effective; however, in the aggregate, the Patriots only average 1.6 more points per game than Green Bay (please keep Trey Smack in mind while reading this) simply because the Packers pass more. When it’s all said and done, it seems like Maye is still the clear winner here, and I won’t argue with anyone who makes this claim. He’s an outstanding young player. But even so, it’s not quite so cut and dried. Both quarterbacks have suffered this season compared to last season based on factors outside of their control. Love has suffered from a terrible offensive line and running game. Maye has lost Romeo Doubs and AJ Brown for extended periods, and his protection has struggled as well. And for Love, there is the added issue of drops. The Packers have an insane number of drops. Matthew Golden leads the league in drops with 9 , and overall, the Packers lead the league with a drop rate of a robust 7% of targets. Those are balls that Jordan Love has put on target (often for what should be big gains) and just don’t happen. And on the other side, Patriots pass catchers have been some of the most reliable in the league, dropping just 2.5% of targets. Love’s efficiency numbers would be substantially higher with an average number of drops instead of whatever this is. Would it be enough to catch Maye? Ehhh, maybe not, but given how often the Packers are throwing the ball, it would certainly be enough to push the Packers’ offense, in the aggregate, past the Pats. In the end, it doesn’t really matter if Maye is better or if Love is better. I think the real lesson is that quarterbacks really are impacted significantly by their surrounding cast, their volume, and their coaching, and that we can never really truly remove all of that context. Secondarily, it’s important to account for that context when making predictions! I’m not sure that Matthew Golden is going to start catching everything, and I’m worried that Josh Jacobs’ return is going to lead to more pointless running, but there is a path to victory here for Green Bay. Hopefully they take it.

title: Green Bay Packers news: The Packers are asking Jordan Love to do something historically difficult
summary: Jordan Love is putting together one of the best seasons of his career. That’s good timing, because the Packers aren’t making things particularly easy on him. Through eight games, Love leads the NFL with 2,246 passing yards and has thrown 16 touchdowns. He’s on pace for a franchise-record 4,772 passing yards, potentially surpassing Aaron Rodgers’ […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) Jordan Love is putting together one of the best seasons of his career. That’s good timing, because the Packers aren’t making things particularly easy on him. Through eight games, Love leads the NFL with 2,246 passing yards and has thrown 16 touchdowns. He’s on pace for a franchise-record 4,772 passing yards, potentially surpassing Aaron Rodgers’ 2011 season. But there’s a caveat: Love is being asked to overcome problems that few quarterbacks could reasonably be expected to sustain. The Packers are averaging just 60.6 rushing yards per game, the lowest mark in the NFL over the past decade. They’re also responsible for 23 dropped passes, eight more than any other team. Against Carolina, Green Bay managed just 66 rushing yards on 26 carries. Opposing defenses continue to make Love beat them through the air. So far, he has. His development into a quarterback capable of carrying an offense is encouraging, and the team’s 5-3 record reflects that resilience. But there’s a difference between having a quarterback who can overcome adversity and building an offense that consistently puts him in that position. The Packers don’t need Love to do more. They need the rest of the offense to do more for him. So what can change? Unfortunately not much! The trade deadline is approaching, and I suppose there’s a possibility that the Packers acquire a new running back. But given the run blocking the team has displayed this year, how much difference might a better back make? Speaking of the line, it’s possible that their run blocking could improve and that could alleviate some of the issues. But don’t hold your breath there. As for pass catchers… anyone can receive a pass, but it’s catching of the pass. That’s the key. Can the Packers receivers turn that around? In the meantime, I’m choosing to simply marvel at the fact that, through 8 games, Jordan Love seems entirely capable of keeping me entertained on Sundays. It’s extremely impressive given the circumstances, and that will have to do. title: How Jonathan Gannon built a Top-5 Packers defense without Micah Parsons
summary: If you’re reading this, you obviously know that on Aug. 28, 2025, the Green Bay Packers traded defensive tackle Kenny Clark, and first-round picks in 2026 and 2027, to the Dallas Cowboys for the services of transcendent edge-rusher Micah Parsons. And when the 2025 season began, it appeared to foster a major improvement in Jeff […]
full_text: USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co If you’re reading this, you obviously know that on Aug. 28, 2025, the Green Bay Packers traded defensive tackle Kenny Clark, and first-round picks in 2026 and 2027, to the Dallas Cowboys for the services of transcendent edge-rusher Micah Parsons. And when the 2025 season began, it appeared to foster a major improvement in Jeff Hafley’s defense. In the first half of the 2025 season, Green Bay’s defense ranked 10th in DVOA and Parsons was on a tear. Through Week 15 of the 2025 season, he totaled 14 sacks and 79 pressures, looking every bit the force he had been with Dallas. Then, in Week 15 against the Denver Broncos, Parsons suffered a torn ACL, and things quickly fell apart for the Pack on Parsons’ side of the ball — and overall. The previously 9-3-1 Pack lost every game from then on, and their season ended abruptly with a 31-27 Wild Card playoff loss to the Chicago Bears. There wasn’t enough juice without their defensive epicenter to get things done. The Packers fell to 25th in Defensive DVOA in the second half of the season, and a primary reason was pretty clear. With Parsons on the field (669 snaps): 4.87 yards allowed per play EPA/play allowed: -0.048 (favorable for the defense) Pass defense: 367 attempts, 6.29 yards per attempt allowed Run defense: 273 attempts, 4.13 yards per carry allowed 29 sacks, 6 interceptions Without Parsons on the field (469 snaps): 5.31 yards allowed per play EPA/play allowed: +0.09 (unfavorable for the defense) Pass defense: 230 attempts, 6.82 yards per attempt allowed Run defense: 231 attempts, 4.18 yards per carry allowed 8 sacks, 3 interceptions “We just need to get healthy,” Parsons told me on September 16 , three days after the Packers lost their season opener to the Minnesota Vikings, 39-22. “I think once we get healthy, and I’m back on that grass or that turf, we’re going to take it to another level.” Thing is, new defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon couldn’t wait around for Parsons to get healthy. The hope was that he’d be ready by Green Bay’s Week 6 game against the Cowboys, but that didn’t happen. Gannon had to do the best he could with what he had. And the extent to which he’s done that is one of the NFL’s most impressive stories in the 2026 season. The Packers currently rank fourth in Defensive DVOA , and Gannon’s concepts have been profoundly unsettling to their opponents. So, how is Gannon doing so well in a new environment, with players he didn’t know last season? Everything is working at all three levels. Creative pressures help everybody get to the quarterback As you would expect, Gannon is blitzing at a pretty high rate (31.9% this season, 12th-highest in the NFL) to maximize pressure, but Green Bay’s pressure rate of 38.7% is only 18th-highest, per SumerSports. Lukas Van Ness leads the team with five sacks and 28 total pressures. Rookie Dani Dennis-Sutton is second with four sacks, and fellow edge-rusher Brenton Cox Jr. is second with 22 pressures. This isn’t a Murderer’s Row in that regard, but the ways in which Gannon has used his guys up front give those guys an edge. It’s also one reason the Packers have been so effective when they don’t blitz. Per SumerSports: Dropbacks Pass Att Comp Comp % Pass Yds Yds/Att TD INT Sacks Sack Rate % Scrambles Pressure Rate % Passer Rating EPA per Dropback Blitz 103 92 54 58.7 514 5.59 3 3 6 5.8 5 43.7 71.6 -0.2 No blitz 220 192 127 66.1 1253 6.53 7 7 16 7.3 12 36.4 81.4 -0.059 So, how do you generate effective pressure when your pressure rate isn’t that high? In Gannon’s case, he’s been marvelous with his simulated pressure designs. Showing a blitz look and then having supposed blitzers drop into coverage can create mental pressure for a quarterback when you do it right, and the Packers have done it right more often than not. Jonathan Gannon has been great with his simulated pressure concepts this season. When you don't have an alpha dog pass-rusher on the field, you need to scheme it up, and Gannon has a full playbook of deceit to create mental pressure for opposing quarterbacks. pic.twitter.com/Qx65JBJuaN — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) November 3, 2026 Now, imagine Parsons as part of all this skullduggery. The (backup) linebackers can do a bit of everything Gannon thought that he’d have linebackers Edgerrin Cooper (season-ending ruptured Achilles tendon) and Zaire Franklin (hairline shin fracture) full-go, but things happen. Now, Isaiah McDuffie and Ty’Ron Hopper are the primary ‘backers, and Hopper has been a revelation. He made NFC Secret Superstars for Week 8 after a 27-19 win over the Carolina Panthers in which he totaled one sack, four pressures, six solo tackles, three pass breakups, and an interception. Hopper became the first Packers player since Hall of Famer Charles Woodson in 2009 to record three pass breakups, a sack, and an interception in the same game. Anytime you can put yourself in the same conversation as Charles Woodson, that’s obviously a good thing. When Gannon runs all of those sim pressures, he needs linebackers who can both threaten pressure and drop into credible coverage. Hopper certainly has it on the ball, and McDuffie has been an effective starter of late. Ty'Ron Hopper being all historic and whatnot pic.twitter.com/hLgzp4mPiX — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) November 1, 2026 “Ty’Ron Hopper. I can’t say enough great things about him,” Matt LaFleur said after the Panthers game. “The night he had. I think, what? Sack, PBU, interception? What a great performance. I think that’s something that we did see coming more so in the preseason. I can’t say enough about the job that obviously [linebackers coach] Sam Siefkes does with our inside linebackers to get them ready, and I just see a lot of growth from that group. They’re playing really well.” They are, and they jibe with the secondary very well. Evan Williams leads a young, smart defensive backfield Safety Evan Williams made Secret Superstars following Green Bay’s 23-13 Week 6 win over the Cowboys — the one Micah Parsons wasn’t ready for, unfortunately — and that was a game in which Williams, the 2024 fourth-rounder out of Oregon, really put his name out there nationally as one of the NFL’s better players at his position(s). This season, Williams has a sack, nine pressures, 49 solo tackles, 13 stops, and two tackles for loss. In coverage, he’s allowed 11 catches on 20 targets for 79 yards, one touchdown, two interceptions, four pass breakups, and an opponent passer rating of 41.5. That’s all great, but where Williams really shows up in Gannon’s defense is how well he plays to all three levels of the defense. Whether he’s starting at the line of scrimmage and backing up to the deep half in coverage, or running the opposite by coming down for a pressure or a run fit, or maintaining the LOS integrity from the box, there isn’t much Williams can’t do right now. And when you have one of those players, it allows you to be as multiple as you’d like without the breakdowns you see on defenses where the personnel doesn’t quite measure up. The best defenses disguise their intentions pre-snap, but at and after the snap, everything is connected to everything else. The @packers do this very well, and safety Evan Williams is the three-level connector. pic.twitter.com/dsWBxvLvkJ — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) November 4, 2026 “He’s intelligent… I love how Matt says it, ‘if you wanna play like a G, you have to prepare like a G’, and he studies and when you study the way he does, he knows what’s going on,” Gannon said of Williams in late October . “Nothing is catching him by surprise… He’s playing very well right now.” And now, with all that said… here comes No. 1. The first look at Micah Parsons on the practice field: pic.twitter.com/ssbGtNQBTj — Rob Demovsky (@RobDemovsky) November 4, 2026 We all know how potentially explosive LaFleur’s offense can be, but it’s past time to recognize that as the 5-3 Packers progress through the rest of the season, it’s the…

title: Packers-Patriots Preview: Christian Gonzalez defines New England’s defense
summary: Last week, the Carolina Panthers sat in split-safety coverages against the Green Bay Packers, forcing the team to run the football or take checkdown passes routinely — just like their matchup in 2025. While this didn’t stop the Packers’ offense, which still had a 100-yard receiver in Christian Watson despite his in-game trip to the […]
full_text: (Photo by Megan Briggs/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last week, the Carolina Panthers sat in split-safety coverages against the Green Bay Packers, forcing the team to run the football or take checkdown passes routinely — just like their matchup in 2025. While this didn’t stop the Packers’ offense, which still had a 100-yard receiver in Christian Watson despite his in-game trip to the hospital for a rib injury, it did mean that the offense was a lot less explosive than it was in prior weeks. Don’t expect that same strategy from the New England Patriots this week, as it’s not really their identity to sit back and just let offense happen to them, hoping that the opposing team will trip up at some point. According to Next Gen Stats, the Patriots have sent max pressure (six or more pass rushers) with man coverage behind it 37 times already this season, the most in the league. On those looks, they’ve posted five sacks and allowed just 14 completions on 31 pass attempts (45 percent) for 123 yards (4.0 yards per attempt), with one interception and no touchdowns surrendered. The overall conversion rate on those players is 21.6 percent, which is the best mark in the league in these situations. In contrast, New England has only sent 13 of these “max pressure” looks out of zone in 2026, surrendering 9 of 13 in the air for 131 yards (10 yards per attempt) and a touchdown. In short, the Patriots’ man coverage looks have been better for them than zone coverage looks this year, especially when they’re trying to speed quarterbacks up. Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez, their All-Pro defender, helps the team unlock that man coverage identity when so many other NFL teams are leaning out of the man coverage game. When Gonzalez has been on the field, the team has played man coverage on 39 percent of their defensive snaps, compared to just 29 percent when he’s not in the game. Packers quarterback Jordan Love has done his most damage this year against the blitz when he’s had either Christian Watson or Matthew Golden in one-on-one looks, but unlike a lot of the teams Green Bay has played this year, the Patriots are just as comfortable playing man as they are playing zone, even behind a blitz. Gonzalez travels, as he’s followed around specific receivers in man coverage at least 10 times in three separate games, a number that leads the NFL. For perspective, neither Watson nor Golden has been seen man coverage 10 times by a single defender in a single game this entire season. Something has to break here. This is going to be the most important matchup of Sunday’s game, by far. The only question is whether Gonzalez will travel with a receiver and which one of the Packers’ deep threats it will be.

title: Time for Texans to put their money where their mouth is…
summary: We’ve been hearing it over and over for the last 2 years: the Texans want to play hat-on-hat, smash-mouth football. An aggressive, “establish the run” sort of offense that the Erhardt-Perkins offensive scheme flourishes with, when done properly. Unfortunately, offensive coordinator Nick Caley and offensive line coach/run game coordinator Cole Popovich have been unable to […]
full_text: We’ve been hearing it over and over for the last 2 years: the Texans want to play hat-on-hat, smash-mouth football. An aggressive, “establish the run” sort of offense that the Erhardt-Perkins offensive scheme flourishes with, when done properly. Unfortunately, offensive coordinator Nick Caley and offensive line coach/run game coordinator Cole Popovich have been unable to pull this rabbit out of their (un)imaginary hat. Last year, it was easy to point the finger at the mysterious injury/illness/medical foot condition of running back Joe Mixon. To rectify this in the off-season, general manager Nick Caserio traded for former Detroit Lion RB2 David Montgomery, who was promptly injured. Now, it all seems to fall on Woody Marks and a jumbo-package of basic run plays that wouldn’t fool the local High School defense, much less an NFL one. Marks is a great runner, but not a one-man Houston Texans running back depth chart. Despite mountains of evidence to make a case that the coaching is largely to blame, both in what the coaches are teaching the players and what plays Caley is calling, head coach Demeco Ryans seems to think the players are at fault, 100%. Well, if it’s a player problem, then here’s a player solution: Update: Teams have reached out to the Ravens regarding a potential trade for RB Derrick Henry, per league source. pic.twitter.com/4B1AViI8Lo — NFL Talk (@NFL_Talk_Sports) November 4, 2026 While Derrick Henry might be 33 and nearing the end of the road, he still has plenty of gas in the tank. And, on a team with Woody Marks and C.J. Stroud, he wouldn’t have to carry the entire load like he’s currently expected to do with the Baltimore Ravens. An aging lion is still lethal and threatening. Even if only the threat of him is enough to make opposing defenses fear the run some of the time. Derrick Henry on if he feels he needs to carry the team with all the injuries at QB: pic.twitter.com/H0s6QMvuHN — Jamison Hensley (@jamisonhensley) November 2, 2026 So far in 2026, Henry has carried the ball 158 times for 632 yards at a 4.0 yard per carry average. He’s also caught 12 of 14 passes for 75 yards. All this has added 9 touchdowns to the Ravens 2026 totals. Enough to put him in 7th place in the current running back Top 10. Meaning, an aging Henry is still better than most of the running backs in the NFL. 9 more touchdowns on the Texans season moves them to 5-2, if not 6-1. While other teams, such as the New York Giants, might go hard in the paint to get Henry, the Texans are at make-or-break time for the current regime. We’ve already gone over , ad nauseum, how bad Caserio, Ryans, Caley, defensive coordinator Matt Burke and Popovich have squandered the off-season hype and fan goodwill. Continuing down the current path of failure leads to the McNair’s having no choice but to fire some or all of them. Often in these situations, embattled GMs and coaches will make Hail Mary trades to attempt to salvage a make or break, one player away season. With Caserio’s history of trade wheeling and dealing, it’s quite possible that this could, and will happen. MSN.com According to ESPN’s Dan Graziano, fans should keep an eye on Henry as the trade deadline approaches. With this season spiraling out of control, Baltimore could move him to a contender for some draft picks. “If he isn’t in Baltimore’s plans beyond this year, the Ravens could find themselves fielding offers over the next week,” Graziano wrote. “Henry’s base salary this year is just $1.255 million (he made the rest of this year’s $14 million via bonuses the Ravens have already paid), so he’d be extremely easy for another team to absorb onto its cap.” Where the problem really lies is trade compensation to the Ravens. Rumors swirl it will take at least a 2nd round pick and a player or later round pick to draw Henry away. Houston currently holds a 1st, 3rd, 4th and 3 – 7th round picks in 2027, and their normal complement in 2028. Odds are Baltimore won’t take a 3rd to keep Henry in the AFC, when the Giants might easily offer up a 2nd. Baltimore is lacking in one key area though, quarterback. And, Houston has arguably one of the best QB2s in the NFL with Davis Mills. Could the Texans offer Mills, a 3rd and 7th to land Henry? Giving up Stroud’s backup is likely unwise in a league where injuries are “when’s” not “ifs”, but failing to hire better offensive coaches has put the team in this position. This also comes down to tonight’s game. The Jacksonville Jaguars are in Baltimore preparing to play the Ravens on Thursday Night Football. If the Ravens win Henry likely stays put. If they lose, Caserio is on the clock. If the Glitter Kitties win, that continues their grip on the current AFC South lead. If they lose, Houston can move closer to taking that lead away – assuming they beat the Los Angeles Chargers this Sunday. Do we root for the Jags to lose so Texans schedule presents an easier path to the division title or for the Ravens to fall so Caserio has a better open door for getting one of the only true smash-mouth running backs they can grab at this juncture? Why they didn’t really go after Henry when he left the BESFs is a bit of a mystery, but now might be their chance to rectify that. God knows Henry has certainly proven he can run in NRG… From 2024: Derrick Henry is on the Texans radar, according to @AaronWilson_NFL 👀 pic.twitter.com/vxTkrDDRv4 — Nick Schwager (@nick__schwager) March 12, 2024 If the Texans braintrust is really locked on their hat-on-hat, jumbo package run game, then trading for Henry is a move they have to explore, and sacrifice to make.

title: Value of Things: By the Numbers
summary: In this edition we usually take a look at the offense or defense as a whole. This time we will take a look at C.J. Stroud specifically. We are going to do this in three parts. The first way is to simply take the best per game statistics that we have (since he has had […]
full_text: Ohio State quarterback C.J. Stroud hugs his mother, Kim, after his workout on the Buckeyes' pro day. CJ Stroud | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co In this edition we usually take a look at the offense or defense as a whole. This time we will take a look at C.J. Stroud specifically. We are going to do this in three parts. The first way is to simply take the best per game statistics that we have (since he has had his bye week) and compare that to the other quarterbacks in the league. I should pause here for a moment to lay out some ground rules. The first ground rule is that they have to have qualified with minimal playing time so both Lamar Jackson and Baker Mayfield didn’t make the cut. Secondly, any placeholder quarterback wasn’t considered with the exception of Kirk Cousins. That left us with the 22 quarterbacks. We are looking at yards per game, net yards per attempt, touchdown percentage, interception percentage, completion percentage, and quarterback rating. We will take Stroud’s rankings in each of these categories and come up with a composite ranking. That will be the first part of the test. Stroud’s Numbers Yards per game: 266.7 (6th) Net yards per attempt: 6.8 (10th) Completion percentage: 64.8 (12th) Touchdown %: 4.5 (15th) Interception %: 0.4 (2nd) QB Rating: 100.7 (8th) Composite Ranking: 8.83 In other words, based on these rankings and these rankings alone, we could classify Stroud as a top ten quarterback. Naturally, there are all kinds of caveats we have to look at before making a declarative statement. First, none of these numbers include running numbers which obviously will tip the scales for the Josh Allens of the world. Secondly, there are those that would question the efficacy of such rankings because talent is not equally distributed and let’s just say that coaching know how is not equally distributed. However, ESPN published their report on the negotiations in the offseason and they would seem damning now that Stroud is almost half way into the season. So, we are looking at similarity scores through two different means. The first round is to simply take the two quarterbacks closest to Stroud in the composite rankings. I think everyone will find this one fascinating. Similarity Score One The two quarterbacks most similar to Stroud in composite ranking are Drake Maye and Caleb Williams. As luck should have it, those are the two quarterbacks most likely to get extensions this next offseason. So, it will be a race to the bank so to speak as the first contract is likely to inform the other two. The third quarterback on the list was Josh Allen, but since these numbers didn’t include his rushing statistics, that comparison would be pretty moot if we really tried to make it stick. Similarity Score Two The second way to do similarity scores is to look category by category and identify the three quarterbacks in each category that come closest to his score. Obviously, if we see the same names multiple times then we could also surmise that they are similar to Stroud. If we see Williams or Maye on the list then it strengthens the notion that those three quarterbacks are similar. Yards Per Game: Matthew Stafford, Kirk Cousins, Bryce Young Net Yards per attempt: Caleb Williams, Jordan Love, Matthew Stafford Completion percentage: Dak Prescott, Deshaun Watson, Kirk Cousins Touchdown percentage: Aaron Rodgers, Dak Prescott, Sam Darnold Interception percentage: Jaden Daniels, Jared Goff, Caleb Williams Quarterback rating: Patrick Mahomes, Kirk Cousins, Drake Maye I think the names are repeated enough to give us something to go on. Kirk Cousins appears three times, Matthew Stafford, Dak Prescott, and Caleb Williams all appear twice. The rest only appear once. So, one could credibly claim that Stroud is most similar statistically to Kirk Cousins. Since Williams is a holdover from the other list then we can add his name as an obvious second choice. Ramifications This is where context comes into play. The Las Vegas Raiders and Chicago Bears are two of the best offensive teams in the NFL with two gifted offensive head coaches. The fact that Stroud is in the same conversation as them is a testament to him and not necessarily meant as a shot. Certainly if one looks at the pedigree of Williams and the accomplishments (regular season) of Cousins then it is easy to see what could be possibly if Stroud were given that mythical long term contract. Of course, the other half of that is having an offensive line and coaching staff that can take full advantage of his talents. This is where quarterback ratings become part science and part art. Where would he rank if he were not addled with Nick Caley and this offensive line? Ninth seems low in that scenario. Maybe he brushes up against the top five. He probably settles in at somewhere around sixth or seventh if he had a Ben Johnson type at offensive coordinator. Is that worth 60 or 65 million dollars? That is obviously the 65 million dollar question. Ironically, while much has changed through his play this season, this point really hasn’t. If you are going to continue to play ball control and put training wheels on Stroud then he probably isn’t worth that money. It has nothing to do with him per se. If you were to put the same shackles on Patrick Mahomes then you’d probably reach the same conclusion. If they install an offense that takes full advantage of his abilities then he definitely is worth the money. That all comes down to DeMeco Ryans and whether he can fully admit that you aren’t a smash mouth football team. Time will tell if that ever happens.
author: Scott Barzilla

title: Believe it or not, but the Colts can turn their season around
summary: Hear me out. I fully get why anyone would think the season is over for the Indianapolis Colts. To be honest, most of this article will be used to convince even myself otherwise. You have to consider that schedules aren’t balanced for this to work. Think back to last year, and look at the first […]
full_text: Hear me out. I fully get why anyone would think the season is over for the Indianapolis Colts. To be honest, most of this article will be used to convince even myself otherwise. You have to consider that schedules aren’t balanced for this to work. Think back to last year, and look at the first half of this year. Outside of the Tennessee flub, every other game the Colts lost was against a tough team. Things are starting to shift in the other direction and provide a tiny bit of hope. The Colts have six losses against opponents with a 28-19 record. Take out the disastrous Titans game and that record moves to 27-12. That’s a tough start. Now, let’s look at the back half. It sits at 29-37-1, and over the next six games, it’s only 13-31-1. That’s a far cry from 27-12. Yes, there are some caveats. The Colts are also not a great team, and they would essentially need to win 5-6 of those contests. The Bengals, Browns???, and Jaguars sit as formidable opponents in the last three weeks of the season too. It won’t be easy, but it’s not impossible either. We witnessed 2025 as the Colts started red hot. Why? A soft schedule provided a false sense of security. It got much harder, and the wheels fell off. This season is the inverse. This is where the Colts need to make their move. Three home games before the bye and a date on the road in Houston are up next. This is it. Four wins put them back at .500, which is somewhere no one can imagine at this point. Even a loss has them dangling by a thread at 5-7, but two road games against the Eagles and Titans after the bye aren’t that daunting. Is it going to be tough? Absolutely. It won’t be Herculean, though. It can be done. The schedule is rounding into the perfect ripeness to get back on track. Things might be very different come the end of November. Then again, a loss against Dallas might be all it takes to permanently flatline this season. All I’m saying is there’s a chance.

title: Colts RB Jonathan Taylor offers cryptic response on possible trade request from Indianapolis
summary: Per The Athletic’s James Boyd, Indianapolis Colts star running back Jonathan Taylor offered a cryptic response when asked whether he has recently requested a trade from the organization, only essentially indicating that “the hay is in the barn now, and he’s preparing for the Dallas Cowboys at home”: As recently as last week, Taylor indicated […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 27: Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts looks on before the game against the Houston Texans at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images Per The Athletic’s James Boyd, Indianapolis Colts star running back Jonathan Taylor offered a cryptic response when asked whether he has recently requested a trade from the organization, only essentially indicating that “the hay is in the barn now, and he’s preparing for the Dallas Cowboys at home”: #Colts RB Jonathan Taylor was asked if he’s requested a trade. His answer was unclear. “At this point, the hay is in the barn now. We’re preparing for the #Cowboys . We got a home game. After last week, nothing else matters. We just gotta give these fans a win.” pic.twitter.com/hzFbDnNFOO — James Boyd (@RomeovilleKid) November 5, 2026 As recently as last week, Taylor indicated that he hadn’t requested a trade from the Colts, despite a few of his (former) teammates such as DeForest Buckner and Josh Downs presumably going down that road as of late. While it was reported that the Colts haven’t been actively shopping Taylor around the league and potentially consider him a cornerstone of their ongoing rebuild to build around and complement, there are a number of heavily interested league suitors, and Indianapolis is clearly listening to prospective offers. It’s been reported that the Colts are hoping for at least a ‘Christian McCaffrey-esque draft capital package”, and who knows, maybe even a first round pick to recoup some of the value lost from losing their own 2027 first round pick, which is a likely Top 5 pick that now belongs to the New York Jets as part of the surrendered trade package from last year’s Sauce Gardner trade deadline deal. At any rate, Taylor is one of the last key remaining longstanding veteran pillars of the Colts prior regime and remains a Top 5 player at the running back position—albeit an elite player who turns 28-years-old in January and realistically may only have 2-3 prime seasons left at a running back position that isn’t forgiving for 30-year-olds. That may be at best, the amount of time that it takes for the Colts to complete an expedited and successful rebuild (if all goes according to plan) given they don’t have a first round pick in 2027, still lack a viable franchise quarterback answer, and the current sad state of their diminished roster collectively (thanks, Chris Ballard!). There’s probably some sentiment for Taylor, who’s a strong franchise Ring of Honor candidate some day, remains on a Pro Football Hall of Fame track, and trails only Edgerrin James as the franchise’s all-time leading rusher in yards and carries, while already holding the record for most rushing touchdowns in Colts history. It won’t be an easy decision to make either way, unless the Colts are blown away, and it appears as though it may take that type of “king’s ransom” running back package for Indianapolis to seriously entertain moving Taylor.
