title: Just how hard is the rest of the Steelers’ schedule?
summary: The Steelers are 6-2 and hold sole possession of the AFC North as they enter a Week 9 bye. But stop me if you’ve heard this one before: The second half of Pittsburgh’s schedule looks quite a bit harder than the first. Or does it? After facing the Falcons, Patriots, Bengals, Browns (twice), Colts, Buccaneers […]
full_text: Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images | Getty Images The Steelers are 6-2 and hold sole possession of the AFC North as they enter a Week 9 bye. But stop me if you’ve heard this one before: The second half of Pittsburgh’s schedule looks quite a bit harder than the first. Or does it? After facing the Falcons, Patriots, Bengals, Browns (twice), Colts, Buccaneers and Saints before the bye, Pittsburgh has played in four games where its opponent would have a winning record at midseason, losing to New England (now 5-3), defeating Cincinnati (now 5-2), and splitting its series with Cleveland (5-3). After the bye, the Steelers face the Bengals again, along with the Eagles (2-6), Broncos (6-2), Texans (2-5), Jaguars (5-2), Ravens (4-4; twice), Panthers (3-4) and Titans (1-7). At first glance, it’s a harder stretch than the first. The Jaguars, and maybe even the Broncos, are better than anyone the Steelers have played so far. The Panthers, despite their poor record, might be the best team in a hapless NFC South lineup. The Texans are 2-1 over the last three weeks despite a 0-4 start to the year, and we all know the Ravens will play the Steelers tough no matter the circumstances. But that group of teams looks weaker than it did before the season started, no? Of the Steelers’ final nine opponents, only three currently have winning records. (Although it’s worth mentioning two matchups against the currently-.500 Ravens). And if we compare the combined midseason winning percentages of the Steelers’ first eight opponents (0.484) to their last nine (0.471), it’s incredibly close. Similarly, while the Steelers didn’t face starting quarterbacks against the Falcons and Buccaneers earlier this season, they won’t either for the upcoming Eagles game ( likely Joe Milton under center ) and at least one of the Ravens games ( likely Jacoby Brissett until Lamar Jackson possibly returns ). Of course, there are far more factors in play than just records and starting quarterbacks — and it’s an unfortunate truth of football that all the teams mentioned in this article will likely have some new, meaningful injuries between now and Week 18. And while the Steelers have the same number of games in Pittsburgh (four) in each half of the season, it’s worth noting that the team’s next five matchups are outside of the usual 1 p.m. EST Sunday time slot. You could definitely argue the Steelers’ second-half schedule is going to be more difficult than the first; I probably would. But the difference isn’t as extreme as you might expect. That’s good news for the Steelers, who already have a 77% postseason probability per NFL.com , currently the AFC’s third seed at 6-2. Pittsburgh’s road to the playoffs remains a promising one entering the bye week.

title: Why Drew Lock is about to take the Seahawks starting QB job for good
summary: (Editor’s note: Everyone please welcome back Michael Thompson to the Field Gulls staff! He was with us all of last season and is returning for at least the rest of this season) For the second straight game against the Arizona Cardinals, Sam Darnold will be on the sidelines injured, while backup Drew Lock will be […]
full_text: (Editor’s note: Everyone please welcome back Michael Thompson to the Field Gulls staff! He was with us all of last season and is returning for at least the rest of this season) For the second straight game against the Arizona Cardinals, Sam Darnold will be on the sidelines injured , while backup Drew Lock will be tasked with helping the Seahawks get an important divisional win. After Monday night’s debacle, a mauling at the hands (paws?) of the new NFC favorites in Chicago, it seems to be fair to question so much about a team that is less than nine months removed from winning the Super Bowl. Is Brian Fleury the right guy to be running this offense? Why can’t the Seahawks run the football? Why can’t anyone get open other than Jaxon Smith-Njigba? How was the defense able to be so easily pushed around by Ben Johnson’s Bears? Should the Seahawks make more trades, or are they too far behind Chicago and San Francisco? There’s a million questions that need and will be answered over the coming days and weeks, but there’s two that I think could potentially answer all of these questions. Was Sam Darnold just soft benched? And does Drew Lock ever give the job back? After a somewhat of a roller coaster 2025 season in Seattle that saw Darnold lead the league in turnovers, but also orchestrate one of the best offenses in football, Sam had his fairytale ending. A crazy fourth quarter comeback to walk-off the Los Angeles Rams in week 16 helped propel the Seahawks to the division title and top seed. From there you know the story, as Sam played the best football of his life against the 49ers and outdueled MVP Matt Stafford en route to a Super Bowl Championship . Those are special memories that we will cherish and cherish Sam forever for. We also have to acknowledge that 2026 Sam is not the same quarterback we saw last year. Suffering some type of serious glute injury on the fifth play of the season , there have been moments of brilliance and immense talent from Darnold, but it has been clouded by more turnovers, a complete regression in pocket awareness, and an overall lack of that gunslinger swagger that made Sam so beloved in Minnesota and Seattle. I don’t know if it is the injuries, the personnel changes, or not having Klint Kubiak around to be his guide, but this version of Sam is hesitant, and he doesn’t believe in himself. I hate to say it, but his level of play looks closer to Jets Sam Darnold than anything he’s put on tap the past two seasons. He’s clearly not healthy, but I can’t help but wonder if his confidence, in both his offensive line and Brian Fluery, is shot. Whenever this type of situation happens with a QB, John Schneider and Mike Macdonald can do one of two things. They can fire Fluery and try to recreate an environment as close to last year as possible for Sam, or they can have Sam take a seat on the bench. Benching Sam would have sent shockwaves through the NFL, and would bring all sorts of negative attention and drama to a team that needs to figure itself out as quickly as possible. But if Sam is not 100%, could they try to find themselves more stable footing on offense, while Sam could get right? I think we’re seeing a soft benching. With the Seahawks likely favored over the Cardinals at home and essentially a home game next week at Las Vegas before the bye, this could give Darnold three weeks to get right, physically and mentally, while the Seahawks believe they can stay alive as their playoff hopes feel like they’re fading fast. Enter Drew Lock’s opportunity Drew Lock was put in one of the toughest positions in week one. You’re the backup to the defending Super Bowl winning QB, and in the first two minutes, he’s hurt and you’re going in, against a pissed off New England Patriots team and the entire football world watching. His first half was ugly, but once he and the team settled in, we saw a version of Lock that we had not seen before. After nearly giving the game away on a duck to Christian Gonzalez, Drew Lock was an efficient game manager, going 16/22 for 187 yards and the massive 4th down touchdown find to JSN. He also had a huge 14-yard scramble on his final drive of the game that should have ended the game if not for penalties. His pocket awareness and mobility allowed plays to develop a bit more for a rookie offensive coordinator, and the championship defense held firm to be a contender in New England. Against the Cardinals on the road, Lock once again looked comfortable and played his best game ever as a Seahawk. In the desert, Drew went 19/26 for 235 yards and three touchdowns (all to JSN). It was honestly an Apex Alex Smith performance from Lock, as he achieved his two most basic functions: don’t turn the ball over and feed JSN. In what ended up a 31-7 win that was very similar to what the Bears just did to Seattle , Lock could have done even more damage if not for turnovers and drops. Fair or not, the Seahawks had some of their best running in the small sample size with Lock running the show. Pair an average running game with a QB that was 15/15 under center and 13/13 in play action during his 7+ quarters of play, and you have a team that is going to find a way to take care of the ball and squeeze the life out of their opponents. Seattle is currently 15th in scoring at 23.1 ppg and 7th in scoring defense at 19.9 ppg. When you look back to last year, the offense is nearly a touchdown worse (28.4) while the defense is giving up almost an extra field goal a game (17.2). They’re not as dominant this year, and the turnovers carry more weight than last year. This team can get back into the hunt and hope to make the playoffs, but they cannot be fourth in the league at 14 turnovers and a -1 turnover differential. Sam could not fix this problem, while Drew never showed it was a problem in his small sample size. With Drew at the helm, the Seahawks were 2-0, and people were talking about the Seahawks as the prohibitive favorite to repeat. Lock had proven the floor was high because our backup could be a very good QB in this current environment, but Sam’s ceiling made the decision to go back easy. Now, the game has changed. As Sam (however you want to divide up the blame pie) and this offense have shit the bed, Drew will be asked once again to come in and help keep the season alive. If Lock plays well, just competent top 13-15 guy level of football, the Seahawks are going to go 2-0. If the Seahawks get to 4-0 with giving the Rock to Lock, we will have the most fascinating bye week in team history. With a potentially season-defining road contest at San Francisco after the bye, will the team really take the ball out of Drew’s hands, if he’s undefeated? I have no doubt the team loves Sam, but there’s no world in which the locker room will allow a switch once again, especially if the team is undefeated with Lock under center. It’s a big if, IF the Seahawks went into Levi’s Stadium again, and came out victorious with Drew Lock, then the job will be his until the Seahawks are eliminated or are playing on Super Bowl Sunday. And this team still has that potential in them. This is still a championship defense. JSN absolutely has the ability to carry a team on a deep playoff run. They just need a quarterback that can channel the ghosts of Jeff Hostetler, Trent Dilfer, Brad Johnson, and Nick Foles. It feels crazy that we have gotten to this point with Sam and Drew, but with the ball in Lock’s hands, I think there’s a real chance he doesn’t give it back, and we have seen the last snaps of Sam Darnold at quarterback for the Seattle Seahawks.

title: The Seahawks are living in the worst of both red zone worlds
summary: The Seattle Seahawks are 4-4, just lost by 17 points to the Chicago Bears on Monday night, yet still have a +26 point differential. Turnovers have obviously been a huge factor in three of their four defeats, but a season-long issue for Seattle’s offense and defense has been seemingly unshakeable. Neither unit is getting the […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks are 4-4, just lost by 17 points to the Chicago Bears on Monday night, yet still have a +26 point differential. Turnovers have obviously been a huge factor in three of their four defeats, but a season-long issue for Seattle’s offense and defense has been seemingly unshakeable. Neither unit is getting the job done in the red zone. Seattle’s offense is one of the worst in the red zone Seattle’s offense ranks a dismal 29th in red zone touchdown percentage, scoring just 13 TDs on 28 trips. If you look at points per red zone trip, which obviously includes field goals, Seattle still ranks 29th. For whatever reason, even though red zone performance is supposedly a high-variance statistic, the Seahawks have not once fielded a top-16 offense in points per red zone possession in the post-Russell Wilson era. This is currently the worst Seahawks offense in the red zone since 2016, when they had a mostly injured Wilson at quarterback, a heavily injured running back unit, and an offensive line that was a total horror show. While the red zone encompasses the 20-yard line and in, there’s an observation I’ve made throughout the season with Brian Fleury’s playcalling. When the Seahawks are faced with a goal-to-go situation, Fleury’s default move is to run the ball to mixed (at best) results. I’m not joking: 12 runs to 1 pass. The pass was a touchdown to Cooper Kupp in the hurry-up offense against the Washington Commanders, by the way. I present to you every Seahawks goal-to-go play on 1st down this season, with the exception of a kneeldown against the Chargers. The Seahawks are the only team in the NFL with a 1st down run rate above 90% in goal-to-go situations. pic.twitter.com/ciZqYtv2TH — Mookie Alexander (@mookiealexander) November 5, 2026 No other team (at least using Stathead play-by-play data ) is more run-heavy on first-and-goal than Seattle. Only the New York Giants and Cleveland Browns have thrown it once on first-and-goal. Last season, the Seahawks had a pass-run ratio of 14:19 on first-and-goal, and while the red zone offense was also lackluster under Klint Kubiak, they were not extraordinarily predictable. The first-and-goal runs are not the main reason Seattle is a poor red zone offense, but it’s certainly a factor. We’ve seen very little play-action in the red zone on any down, and the Seahawks roster generally lacks a true “go up and get it” receiving target. That last bit is mostly opinion, but you can probably count the number of high-point catches made by Seahawks receivers on one hand this year—Jaxon Smith-Njigba included. It’s not a strength of this roster and it has to be something Seattle considers when it inevitably examines how to improve the offense next season. Seattle’s red zone defense is the worst in the NFL This part is stunning. The Seahawks defense as a whole is still playing very well, but they’re losing in the key situational areas at an alarming rate. They rank 32nd in red zone efficiency, conceding touchdowns on 15 of 18 possessions. Last year they were the fifth-best at preventing red zone touchdowns, and now they’re just bleeding them every trip. By FTN’s DVOA , they are last in red zone pass, red zone rush, and goal-to-go situations. This probably would matter less if the Seahawks offense wasn’t performing so poorly regardless of where they are on the field, but Seattle is costing themselves wins with these weekly disparities. The Seahawks' defense is addressing its biggest Achilles' heel from Monday night: red-zone efficiency. The Seahawks broke down the team's struggles inside the 20 and what needs to change to hold opponents to three instead of six. #Seahawks #SeahawksNation #GoHawks #NFL #Seattle pic.twitter.com/gzov7YoRvK — KING 5 Sports (@KING5Sports) November 4, 2026 And while this is a post about the red zone, the Seahawks defense is the worst 4th down unit in the NFL, giving up 10 of 11 conversions. It’s not the only area where they’ve fallen off. The Seahawks defense on a macro level is still elite, but there are margins where there's a clear dropoff that explains why they're not as good as last year. 3rd down EPA/rush is 29th after being 1st last year. RZ woes tie-in. 2nd and short DVOA is 19th. 2nd and Med is 15th. — Mookie Alexander (@mookiealexander) November 4, 2026 Seattle became Super Bowl champions last season by “chasing edges” and winning the games within the game. The little things that add up to victories. They’re getting their asses kicked in the margins, and if the red zone performances don’t improve soon, they’ll find themselves missing the playoffs for the fourth time in six seasons.

Two unlikely 49ers — a fullback and a party animal — just made team’s 10-year wall (paywall) “ Shanahan and Lynch joked that they started pronouncing his last name as “huge check” when deciding how high they’d go to sign him. “There were numerous suitors for him, and at some point Kyle and I said, ‘Wow. This is getting real,’” Lynch said after the signing. The hefty price tag drew criticism then. Under the headline, “2017 NFL free agency, worst contracts so far,” NFL.com wrote that “agents smelled blood in the water with new general manager John Lynch and knocked him around at the negotiating table.” Juszczyk’s contract again garnered attention when, following the 2024 season, the 49ers released him in a cost-cutting move before bringing him back four days later. That brief estrangement falls under the 10-year wall’s 10-second rule — it technically happened but officially didn’t count. The next face on the wall is George Kittle’s…..The 49ers have used 21 personnel — two backs (one of whom is Juszczyk) and one tight end — more than any other team since 2017. And it’s absolutely fitting that Juszczyk switched lockers this year so he could be next to the other two players in that 21 personnel combination, Kittle and Christian McCaffrey. “I’m in my 14th season of the NFL,” Juszczyk said when asked about his migration to the other side of the locker room. “I don’t want it to be the end, but at some point it will be. So I figured in these last couple of years, I really wanted to enjoy things and be surrounded by my best friends.” Kawakami: The 49ers are rested, restocked, and ready for a late-season run (paywall) “That’s a green-flag signal: Time to put the pedal all the way down. “It’s telling you that they believe that it could be something special,” Trent Williams said in the locker room before practice on Wednesday. “Obviously, we believe. “But … you know, somebody can tell you they love you all day, but when they show you … They’re showing us by bringing in more people like [Buckner] that can change the scope of the franchise.” Yes, the 49ers would be feeling good no matter what after going 6-1 to start this season, getting plenty of rest during last weekend’s bye, and knowing that Nick Bosa and maybe some other important players will be back for Sunday’s game against the Raiders at Levi’s Stadium. But long NFL seasons always seem shorter and more exciting when a front office can add some electricity with a big trade. Bringing back Buckner, who starred for the 49ers before he was traded away in 2020, was the perfect boost.” Is DeForest Buckner’s ‘nostalgic’ trade return the final piece for the 49ers? “Bosa mentioned the idea of trading for Buckner to coach Kyle Shanahan a couple of months ago. Kittle and Juszczyk discussed it with other teammates and personnel types, remaining in contact with Buckner while he was in Indy. Buckner also heard directly from Greenlaw and Samuel at various points. That group holds a bond that Buckner said will “never be broken” from their previous time together. A common theme in the conversations that group has had over the years? Their shared unfinished business, not just from the Super Bowl loss but in the time that has elapsed since. In some ways, it would make getting over the hump and claiming the franchise’s sixth Lombardi Trophy this season even sweeter. “It would make a good documentary if we did it,” Bosa joked. “Obviously having him back … we want to do it this year.” A 49ers trade deadline wishlist: 7 players who could help win a Super Bowl “ WR Chimere Dike, Titans: Allow me to pull one completely out of left field. But let’s say the 49ers’ plan to get better at receiver is to wait for the returns of Demarcus Robinson (which feels sooner rather than later) and De’Zhaun Stribling (which feels later rather than sooner). Or let’s say the 49ers even try to rebuild a bridge with a certain player who is reportedly showing up to work on Friday. Let’s just call it a choose-your-own-adventure to why the 49ers opt not to go after Wilson, Mitchell, or Downs. But maybe they remember what Rashid Shaheed not only did for the Seahawks last season, but what Shaheed did to the 49ers in the playoffs. So what if, instead of going for the big fish at receiver, they instead use the position to solve the long-standing returner issue? The Titans would have no motivation to move Dike with him only in his second season, but with Jeffrey Simmons already gone, it would cause no harm for the 49ers to at least call. If San Francisco does pull the trigger, Dike would become one of the best returners in 49ers history on day one if he continues his pace he’s shown in Tennessee. Dike has 94 kickoff returns so far in his season and a half with the Titans. Only five players in 49ers history (Super Bowl era) have taken more than 75 kickoff returns (Vic Washington, Ted Ginn, Maurice Hicks, Carl Monroe, and Dexter Carter), and Dike’s 25.7 yards per those 94 returns would rank second behind only Washington. The same would apply for punt returns as well. Dike has 34 of those to his name, and while plenty of 49ers (Super Bowl era) have taken at least 30 punt returns (23 to be exact), none are better than Dike’s 15.7 yards per punt return.”

title: Brandon Aiyuk owing the 49ers money could complicate his release
summary: The Ringer’s Tom Pelissero tweeted the following about San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Brandon Aiyuk: Veteran WR Brandon Aiyuk owes the 49ers roughly $13 million in bonus forfeiture — a potential complication in his efforts to secure his release by reporting to the facility Friday. The NFL Management Council and the NFL Players Association are […]
full_text: (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Ringer’s Tom Pelissero tweeted the following about San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Brandon Aiyuk: Veteran WR Brandon Aiyuk owes the 49ers roughly $13 million in bonus forfeiture — a potential complication in his efforts to secure his release by reporting to the facility Friday. The NFL Management Council and the NFL Players Association are both involved in attempting to resolve the situation. The sides could reach an agreement to pay back the money, or it could go to arbitration. But it’s complicated and may take time to resolve. Earlier on Thursday evening, ESPN’s Adam Schefter tweeted that Drew Rosenhaus, Aiyuk’s agent, said, “We will be there tomorrow at 3 pm to meet with the team at the facility. We will put our best foot forward and go from there.” Words are words. These are pros. If Aiyuk is remorseful, it wouldn’t be surprising to see the 49ers brass and locker room accept him with open arms. The more fascinating aspect is what happens with Aiyuk’s contract. Currently, Aiyuk’s under contract through 2028. If he agrees to a restructured contract, likely one that makes him a free agent at the end of the season, why would the Niners part ways with him? The answer would be that both sides believe they have reached a point of no return; there are no actions left to take, and it’s best to part ways with Aiyuk. You could also include Aiyuk in any potential trade—even as a throw-in in place of a draft pick. You might ask why a team would take a risk on a player who hasn’t stepped foot on an NFL field in over two seasons. After it’s all said and done, there’s a plausible outcome where Aiyuk remains on the roster — whether he suits up is another question. But if you’re Kyle Shanahan and you’re looking at a wide receiver depth chart without Mike Evans, Deebo Samuel, potentially Christian Kirk, and another month-plus without De’Zhaun Stribling, you’d think it’d be easy to swallow your pride and take Aiyuk back — provided the locker room does. It feels like there are dozens of reasons to keep Aiyuk, if only for another two months. Best case, he’s your WR2. The worst case is he’s on the scout team, serving as CeeDee Lamb, Justin Jefferson, Jaxon Smith-Njigba, and Malik Nabers in practice over the next month. No outcome would be surprising, which is why we can’t wait to see the update late Friday afternoon. According to Kyle Shanahan, there isn’t any meeting, and his mind is made up: "There's no meeting between [him] and me or our football team on Friday … I'm not even sure what time he's coming in." Kyle Shanahan has completely moved on from Brandon Aiyuk, and he doesn’t anticipate him changing his Friday. (via Dirty Work w/ @Adamcopes & @dpapapops ) pic.twitter.com/fVGZUr5sRj — KNBR (@KNBR) November 6, 2026

title: A 49ers trade deadline wishlist: 7 players who could help win a Super Bowl
summary: The San Francisco 49ers find themselves in a unique spot entering Week 9.  Despite having plenty of needs (pass rusher, secondary, and receiver, to name a few), the 49ers are sitting pretty at 6-1 with a three-game advantage in the loss column in the NFC West. San Francisco has already made a splash and cleaned […]
full_text: (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers find themselves in a unique spot entering Week 9. Despite having plenty of needs (pass rusher, secondary, and receiver, to name a few), the 49ers are sitting pretty at 6-1 with a three-game advantage in the loss column in the NFC West. San Francisco has already made a splash and cleaned up a need by bringing in another old friend in DeForest Buckner, but it can’t hurt the 49ers to make at least another move or two. So here’s my wishlist. Some bigger asks than others, but all within different realms of possibility. If the 49ers can acquire one of the below names, I’ll be happy. Two, I’d be ecstatic. And three or more, I will be thinking about the route for the Super Bowl parade. With the trade deadline right around the corner, here’s my list of the players the 49ers should be looking at: WR Garrett Wilson, Jets Wilson would be that high-end item you put on a wishlist that you know is too pricey to ask for, but you ask for it just in case. It would be hard to imagine the 49ers acquiring a better player at any position (let alone a position of need). The 49ers need a receiver, even with a few coming back from injury over the next few weeks, and Wilson would be the perfect complement across from Mike Evans. Wilson started his career with three consecutive 1,000-yard seasons with Zach Wilson, Mike White, Joe Flacco, Trevor Siemian, and Aaron Rodgers throwing passes to him. Now with Geno Smith as his quarterback, Wilson has 527 yards, pacing for another 1,000-yard season. You can’t blame 49ers fans for imagining what Wilson could be with Purdy as his quarterback. If the price is too high on Wilson, John Lynch and Co. would be smart to inquire about Adonai Mitchell before hanging up on the Jets. S Jessie Bates III, Falcons Your guess is as good as mine if Bates will even be available. Some weeks, Atlanta is good enough to beat a 6-0 49ers team, but others they’re bad enough to lose to a team that doesn’t complete a pass. With the state of the NFC South, you can’t blame the Falcons if they choose to stand pat, but if they are taking calls, Bates would be an ideal trade target for San Francisco. The 49ers have flirted with the idea of Bates, both when he was available for trade when he played for the Bengals and when he was a free agent before he signed with Atlanta. The safety play for the 49ers has been inconsistent this season, and Bates would add stability. Plus there’s already a connection there with Bates playing under 49ers defensive coordinator Raheem Morris in 2023 and 2024, earning a second-team All-Pro nod in the latter year. Bates would be pricey and might need an extension to make a deal work, but he could be a long-term fix to one of the 49ers’ shakier position groups. WR Josh Downs, Colts The Santa Clara-Indianapolis pipeline has already been tapped once with the Buckner trade, so negotiations will be familiar waters for Lynch if he wants to return to that well. If the Jets hold onto Wilson or the 49ers miss out, Downs wouldn’t be a bad consolation. Per NFL Next Gen stats, Downs is a better separator than Wilson, averaging 3.0 yards of separation per route run compared to Wilson’s 2.6. Downs has used that ability to separate to lead the Colts in targets (51), receiving yards (330), and first downs (19). Downs would have a lower cost to acquire than Wilson (although Wilson would be a long-term fix and future replacement for Mike Evans) and would be a clear No. 2 in an injured but crowded wide receiver room. If I had to pick the likeliest player acquired by the 49ers before the trade deadline, I would wager on Downs. DE Josh Sweat, Cardinals An inter-division trade feels unlikely, and the Cardinals can drive the price as high as they want with two more years of control of Sweat, but if the 49ers want to make a huge swing for the fences, Sweat would be the guy. Sweat’s 40.5 sacks career total ranks 12th among all defenders (with only a sack more than Nick Bosa), with 12 sacks in 2025 after signing a four-year, $76.4 million deal with the Cardinals. He hasn’t quite had that success yet this season, recording just three sacks in eight games so far this season. But while his production has been down in 2026, Sweat gives something the 49ers don’t see too often in their pass rushers: a clean bill of health. Sweat has missed only three games since 2021 and hasn’t missed a game since signing with Arizona. The price would be high, but Sweat would be a true 1B to Bosa’s 1A, and if a trade for the Arizona pass rusher is the catalyst for the 49ers’ pass rush becoming elite again, how high is too high? DE Khalil Mack, Chargers A more logical choice would be Mack, but the Chargers don’t seem convinced that an 0-7 start in the AFC West is an impossible task to overcome. If Los Angeles comes to its senses and starts selling, the 49ers should be all over the veteran end. The 49ers have been tied to Mack since he donned the Silver and Black, but the two sides have narrowly missed several times. San Francisco was also interested in Mack when he hit free agency after his time with Chicago,hicago but he went to Los Angeles instead. Maybe the third time will be the charm. Mack isn’t the elite defender he was once, but his 5.5 sacks in 2025 would have led to the 49ers, and his three sacks would be only behind Keion White this season. But unlike in Los An,geles where Mack is the No. 1 pass rusher, he’d be behind Bosa and would draw more favorable matchups than he’s currently facing. San Francisco has flirted with Mack a few times already; maybe the match is finally made before Tuesday’s deadline. DE Jadeveon Clowney, Texans The 49ers have had a need for a second pass rusher for as long as Bosa has been with the franchise. Clowney has been on seven different teams over his 13-year career and four teams over the last four seasons. Somehow, the two have never come together. The Texans enter Week 9 with a 2-5 record, and with Clowney on a one-year deal, there’s no reason to think the veteran can’t be had for cheap. And Clowney has shown he can still go, even on the wrong side of 30. Clowney, at age 33, ranks 12th of all active players with 25.5 sacks after turning 30 , but ranks behind only TJ Watt and Danielle Hunter on the list as the only players in their age-33 season or younger. Clowney to San Francisco has made almost too much sense for too long, and if San Francisco doesn’t land Sweat or Mack, Clowney would absolutely work. WR Chimere Dike, Titans Allow me to pull one completely out of left field. But let’s say the 49ers’ plan to get better at receiver is to wait for the returns of Demarcus Robinson (which feels sooner rather than later) and De’Zhaun Stribling (which feels later rather than sooner). Or let’s say the 49ers even try to rebuild a bridge with a certain player who is reportedly showing up to work on Friday. Let’s just call it a choose-your-own-adventure to why the 49ers opt not to go after Wilson, Mitchell, or Downs. But maybe they remember what Rashid Shaheed not only did for the Seahawks last season, but what Shaheed did to the 49ers in the playoffs. So what if, instead of going for the big fish at receiver, they instead use the position to solve the long-standing returner issue? The Titans would have no motivation to move Dike with him only in his second season, but with Jeffrey Simmons already gone, it would cause no harm for the 49ers to at least call. If San Francisco does pull the trigger, Dike would become one of the best returners in 49ers history on day one if he continues his pace he’s shown in Tennessee. Dike has 94 kickoff returns so far in his season and a half with the Titans. Only five players in 49ers history (Super Bowl era) have taken more than 75 kickoff returns (Vic Washington, Ted Ginn, Maurice Hicks, Carl Monroe, and Dexter Carter), and Dike’s 25.7 yards per those 94 returns would rank second behind only Washington. title: Nick Bosa says ‘I feel great’ and ‘I’m ready to go’
summary: San Francisco 49ers star pass rusher Nick Bosa told reporters, “I feel great” and “I’m ready to go” on Wednesday. Bosa said it’s been tough, but he’s thinking more about the long haul. Bosa spoke about his injury: “It was my other leg. I must’ve had some type of compensation going on, especially in that […]
full_text: (Photo by Santiago Mejia/San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images) San Francisco 49ers star pass rusher Nick Bosa told reporters , “I feel great” and “I’m ready to go” on Wednesday. Bosa said it’s been tough, but he’s thinking more about the long haul. Bosa spoke about his injury: “It was my other leg. I must’ve had some type of compensation going on, especially in that first week back, just kind of trying to push it back with the tendonitis. So, I may have been favoring it a little bit. I was just doing my normal warm-up drills one day, and I tweaked it. Calves are a pretty long process. I’ve never had one, so it took a little longer than I expected. But I don’t even think about it anymore.” Bosa said the calf injury was unrelated to his Achilles. Bosa also mentioned how he could’ve returned earlier. General manager John Lynch was asked about the long-term strategy and plan for Bosa: We don’t take any game for granted, believe me. We only play 17 of these in the regular season, so they all count immensely. I think what we try to do in every situation is, we get our medical people, the doctors, the trainers, and the player involved. And we kinda look at these injuries from every angle involved, and we push ‘em to try to get them back. And when they’re ready, and there are a bunch of objective numbers to hit, to be able to do that. Nick saying that, he probably felt like he could, but I think all working together, we came to the decision that it was best to wait through Atlanta, to get the bye week and then come back. We’re happy we have him back. He’s obviously a difference maker when he’s out there. It will be great to have Nick out there on the field and making a difference like he always does. For as much talk as there is surrounding DeForest Buckner helping out the defensive tackles, Bosa takes immense pressure off Keion White and Romello Height to be every-down players and playing in situations you otherwise wouldn’t. The line will be fresh, but it will also have top-to-bottom talent we haven’t seen since 2022.

We’d have to be really motivated to move Mac in a situation where it makes too much sense in what we had and what we were able to receive for that. But we’re very comfortable with keeping Mac. I don’t… — Nick Wagoner (@nwagoner) November 4, 2026 Here’s what Lynch said about the looming Aiyuk situation: “No. 1, we’ve got a 6-1 football team that we think really has a shot at this year. So, our focus is going to remain on this team. Kyle spoke of that yesterday. Now look, having said that, I have a job to do. And it entails a lot of different things. This is kind of a unique situation. Not one you have. There’s really no playbook. But I always go back to what’s my charge, what’s my job? My job is to look out for the best interest of the 49ers. As such, in this particular situation, we’re working with the NFL management council to navigate through sort of a different situation. It’s fluid; we’re going to kind of leave it at that because I believe it’s the right thing to do. We’ll look for a pathway for both sides that works. How about this for a deal, next week, we can talk a little more in detail about the process. It’s kind of a fluid situation.” Lynch said, “Of course,” when asked if he’d listen to Aiyuk and his agent talk about a possible reunion. “I think everything’s possible. I will say this, we’ve worked with Drew [Rosenhaus] a lot. Drew is a good guy to deal with. He’s reasonable. He’s got integrity. In terms of that, that’s all good. We’ll see how this thing goes. I think we’ll just leave it at that. I’ll have a lot more to share with you in the coming weeks.” Which receivers will be healthy for Week 9? When asked about whether the team is still looking to add a wide receiver, Lynch said: “We will see. We have until Tuesday. We’re excited. We got a couple of guys back. Demarcus Robinson back on the field yesterday. We gotta get him through today’s practice. Thursday’s kind of a grind of a practice. D-Rob was really on a good path. So having him back is a really good sign for us. KhaDarel Hodge came back and joined our practice squad. KhaDarel was playing some really good football. In the coming weeks, we hope to get Deebo and Mike back in the fold as well. We’ve got those guys coming back. As I’ve said consistently, we’ve probably made the move that we were most targeted on in the DeFo move. That may be it. We’re really happy with our team. We’ll see. We’ll keep the phones working until Tuesday until 12:58, I guess, and see what else we can do. And that maybe it. We really love this team.” Lynch was asked a follow-up about Mike Evans: “I don’t know if I’d rule that out; it’s probably likely that he won’t be out there Sunday. What we’re really trying to do there, he’s got that tendonitis that flared up. I think you learn from the history of them, right? Christian had this situation. And every player is different, every situation is different, but you don’t want it to become something that really lingers. So we’re trying to knock it out, such that when he comes back, we’re giving him the best chance to stay back. Mike’s doing really hard to do that.” As for De’Zhaun Stribling: “Strib’s come along well. He had a surgery after Australia. He’s tracking well. I’m not going to get into timelines, but Strib’s coming. He fits in that same mold as the profile of Mike Evans, a tireless worker. So Strib is putting the work in. Hopefully, at the end of this season, we’ll have Strib back in the fold.”

title: Could the 49ers make a deal with the Texans again for a defensive lineman?
summary: The San Francisco 49ers and the Houston Texans have been involved in some business over the past few years. Back in 2024, the 49ers dealt a seventh-round pick for defensive tackle Maliek Collins in a move that worked out for them for a year. Collins was a solid pass-rusher and went on to sign with […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - OCTOBER 04: Defensive tackle Sheldon Rankins #98 of the Houston Texans and defensive end Jadeveon Clowney #90 of the Houston Texans celebrate a defensive stop during the NFL football game between the Houston Texans and Dallas Cowboys on October 4, 2026, at Reliant Stadium in Houston, TX. (Photo by David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers and the Houston Texans have been involved in some business over the past few years. Back in 2024, the 49ers dealt a seventh-round pick for defensive tackle Maliek Collins in a move that worked out for them for a year. Collins was a solid pass-rusher and went on to sign with the Cleveland Browns, where he’s found even more success, recently signing an extension. They’ve also traded seventh-round picks to the Texans for defensive tackle Khalil Davis and offensive lineman Jarrett Patterson in separate trades. Now, could it be time for a fourth deal over the past two years? Heading into the trade deadline, the 49ers already made a splash move, landing DeForest Buckner for a 2027 fourth-round pick to slot in as their new starting defensive tackle. Following that, the 49ers are still actively looking for a pass rusher and a wide receiver, and one of those needs could be filled with a minor trade with the Texans. CBS Sports mocked a trade between the 49ers and Texans for veteran edge rusher Jadeveon Clowney, with the two sides swapping sixth and seventh-round picks in the deal. “The Niners have already given their defensive line a boost by trading for DeForest Buckner, and they should welcome Nick Bosa back into the fold soon, if not this week coming off their bye,” CBS Sports’s Jared Dubin wrote. “But they’re still just 21st in the NFL in pressure rate, according to Tru Media, and they have been dealing with injuries along the defensive front all season. Adding another capable rotational player off the edge could give them an extra boost ahead of a potential playoff run.” In the deal, the 49ers are receiving a 2027 seventh-round pick, while sending out a 2028 sixth-round pick. Clowney has been a name that has popped up in trade conversations this week, as he’s played under 40 percent of the defensive snaps for the Texans and is 33 years old. The 49ers currently have a draft pick in every round but the fourth in the 2027 NFL Draft after the Buckner trade, so they could swap sixths and sevenths this year. But if they’re asked to move a 2028 pick and get a 2027 in return, the deal could make even more sense. And it could make sense for Houston as well, as they currently don’t have a 2028 sixth-round pick. If the 49ers are to look for a pass rusher and a wide receiver, at least one of those moves will have to be cheap. San Francisco doesn’t have any projected compensatory picks coming their way this offseason. So two trades could mean two additional picks from their 2027 war chest gone, leaving them with just four draft picks in the class. A move like this would fill a need while being relatively cheap and adding more leadership to the room with a veteran player who has played in a similar system. Clowney hasn’t been anything special this year, accumulating just nine pressures on 78 pass-rushing snaps. But he’s cheap and a veteran body who can add to a rotation currently ranking 21st in the NFL in pressure rate. That would also allow the 49ers to look for a receiver and still come out fine on the draft capital side going into the offseason.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

summary: The San Francisco 49ers continued their reunion party last week, bringing back former Pro Bowl defensive tackle DeForest Buckner from the Indianapolis Colts six years after trading him away. full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 25: DeForest Buckner #99 of the Indianapolis Colts looks on after the game against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers continued their reunion party last week, bringing back former Pro Bowl defensive tackle DeForest Buckner from the Indianapolis Colts six years after trading him away. Buckner, 32, instantly comes into a starting role in San Francisco alongside Osa Odighizuwa, giving the team some more experience and a veteran presence for a young room of defensive tackles. Buckner was quite productive in 2025, but was on a poor Colts team this season and was expected to be dealt. Naturally, with the need, the 49ers were a perfect fit, and the two sides were able to get a deal done for a fourth-round pick. Now, the defensive tackle will play in his first game with the 49ers since the 2019 Super Bowl against the Kansas City Chiefs, as the team hopes to not only make it back, but win their first championship since 1995. Though it’s been just a week, Buckner’s presence has already been felt in the locker room, according to his teammates. “Oh, it’s awesome,” running back Christian McCaffrey said of Buckner’s arrival. “I think just even in the walkthrough today, you look out there, you got Bosa, you got him out there, all these other [guys]. You’re like, okay, definitely gives you a little boost of confidence. So pumped he’s on our team.” Bosa praised the move, believing it’ll add some needed leadership to the defensive line group for the younger guys. “Yeah, 100%, [we feel a boost],” Bosa said of his former teammate. “I think we needed some leadership, not that we don’t have a couple good leaders in the D-line room, but a guy who’s played this scheme a lot, and we have some emerging young D-tackles, so it’s a perfect fit, really.” Fred Warner echoed the sentiment, noting the impact Buckner had on him back when the two played together for two seasons in 2018 and 2019. “It means everything,” Warner added. “It was special when I found out that we had an opportunity or really when we did get him. That was the guy when I came in as a rookie, I think he was in his 3rd year and he was what everything that we were looking for as a 49er. Just building the culture and the standard here. “He was that, you know, and I learned so much from him early on. And, you know, it was unfortunate, the business side of it, obviously having to be traded to the Colts, but it’s rare you get a second opportunity to come home, right? And so I know he’s excited. I’m excited. He looks phenomenal. And it helps when you have really talented players on the defensive line. It makes my job easier.” Could the 49ers continue to add on the defensive line now? Reports have said they’re still on the look for a pass-rusher, perhaps another veteran to help out a younger room. When speaking to reporters, head coach Kyle Shanahan said the team is still looking for moves that make sense, and a pass rusher might be one of the top needs remaining. While it’s a possibility, Bosa feels quite confident with how the room is stacking up right now. “Oh, I don’t know,” Bosa said when asked about the possibility of another addition. “Yeah, I don’t know. It seems like we’re pretty stacked. [Buckner’s] the blueprint and, and now we get to watch it in person.”

title: How to win, how to lose: Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Chicago Bears week 9 game preview
summary: Anyone watch Monday Night Football? Wow, the Bears look good. Ben Johnson, Caleb Williams, and their Chicago Bears seem like they are on a collision course for a deep playoff run in 2026. So yes, the Bears are hot— Steaming, but so are the Buccaneers. Tampa Bay is coming off two-straight wins, three of their […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - SEPTEMBER 17: Baker Mayfield #6 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers attempts a pass during the first quarter against the Chicago Bears at Raymond James Stadium on September 17, 2023 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Julio Aguilar/Getty Images) | Getty Images Anyone watch Monday Night Football? Wow, the Bears look good. Ben Johnson, Caleb Williams, and their Chicago Bears seem like they are on a collision course for a deep playoff run in 2026. So yes, the Bears are hot— Steaming, but so are the Buccaneers. Tampa Bay is coming off two-straight wins, three of their last four and has seemingly found their new formula for offensive success. Will those good vibes and momentum carry over into the Chicago night on Sunday Night Football? “ Battles are won in the trenches, in the grit and grime of courageous determination. ” Charles R. Swindoll How can the Buccaneers win? Be the line they claim to be. The Chicago Bears are no joke and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers will need to be all the way buttoned up to be able to stay with Chicago in this game. The Bears have a lot of things going for them in 2026, but their most recent addition may be the scariest. Chicago’s highly publicized trade for Jeffery Simmons opened some eyes when they made it. For those who haven’t seen may Titans’ games over the years, Monday night may have opened some more— Simmons is in the elite class of football players in the NFL and after spending years on a losing team, he looks motivated and rejuvenated. The trade for Simmons was an all-in move, the kind of move teams make when they have one goal on their mind— The Bears are a Super Bowl or bust team. The trade paid immediate dividends, Simmons’ first game with Chicago was a watch what I can do performance as he snared a team-leading six tackles (two for a loss) and a sack. For the Buccaneers, this game will be the game where their offensive line needs to prove the last two weeks true. Tampa’s season began horrifically, 0-4, a quarterback injury, and more importantly for the sake of this discussion, an offensive line that was woeful. Tampa Bay’s offensive line came into the season projected to be one of the strongest units on the team, perhaps in the league, depending on who you asked. Through the first four games, the Buccaneers allowed 20 sacks. Baker Mayfield spent most of those first four games running in circles behind the line of scrimmage like Fran Tarkenton, until he ran himself into an injury. In the four since, Tampa’s only surrendered seven sacks with five of the seven coming against the Pittsburgh Steelers. Tampa Bay will be and should be the underdog on Sunday. If there is any chance that an upset is in the cards they will need to protect their quarterback. Baker Mayfield is going to have to attempt more than three passes in this game to lead the team to victory and he will need to be upright to do so. Chicago has an absolute game-wrecker on their defense, he will make his plays— The Bucs can’t expect to wipe Jeffery Simmons out of the game, however, they cannot allow the game to devolve into what fans saw earlier in the season from this offensive line, Baker Mayfield, and the passing game. “ You can’t stop him, you can only hope to contain him .” Dan Patrick How can the Buccaneers lose? Lose contain of Caleb Williams. Caleb Williams might not be a truly great quarterback, though he does seem to be enroute to that status in short order, but he is a truly special athlete. No, he isn’t running 4.2 40’s or leaping 13’ in a broad jump but he is as all around dynamic as they come. One of the issues Tampa Bay might have is Williams simply does not throw interceptions. Caleb has missed some time this year, but he has only thrown one interception— Last year, just seven. Williams’ lack of interceptions isn’t even a Ben Johnson related statistic because dating back two years ago, pre their union, Williams tossed just six while throwing 20 touchdowns for a better than 3:1 touchdown to interception ratio. In his career (three years), Williams has thrown less interceptions than Baker Mayfield did in 2024—Turnovers may be off the table. Another key issue that Caleb Williams presents is his elite management of the pocket. Williams is not a runner, but he is quite mobile. He has a phenomenal ability to majestically glide up, back, or out of the pocket towards free space and away from danger . Todd Bowles and the Buccaneers’ defense will need to work tirelessly to mitigate that on Sunday night. Williams will dagger the Bucs with big plays off script if they let him. Bowles and the Bucs have been somewhat of mixed bag against mobile quarterbacks, different matchups bringing about different results, but Caleb Williams will represent a very unique challenge. Williams is not just looking to move around the pocket to buy time to throw— He isn’t just looking break out of the pocket so that he heave the ball down field on a broken play— He won’t be looking to run outside of contain so that he can scramble for yards to move the chains— Caleb Williams will be looking to do any and all of the above. He is special and he has proven that he can do each and every one of those things on any given play— Meaning, the Buccaneers must be dialed into the details on their rushes, sound in their tackling, and if they are caught lacking and take even just one snap off Williams could gash them for a game changing play. Todd Bowles’ defense has been reliably solid in 2026, as of late they’ve been exemplary. Sunday night’s game against Chicago will be a true test. Caleb Williams has the ability to put a defense on a poster, he and Ben Johnson have left a decent amount of carnation in their wake. Can Tampa Bay contain Caleb Williams and stay off his highlight reel?
author: Will Walsh

title: 3 players the Titans should not trade before the deadline
summary: The NFL trade deadline is approximately five days away (Nov. 10). The Tennessee Titans are obviously sellers at the deadline following their stunning decision to trade superstar defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons to the Chicago Bears in exchange for two first-round picks and an additional fourth-round selection. The Simmons trade poses a question: Who else will […]
full_text: Tennessee Titans running back Tony Pollard (20) carries the ball during the first quarter against the Cleveland Browns at Nissan Stadium in Nashville, Tenn., Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The NFL trade deadline is approximately five days away (Nov. 10). The Tennessee Titans are obviously sellers at the deadline following their stunning decision to trade superstar defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons to the Chicago Bears in exchange for two first-round picks and an additional fourth-round selection. The Simmons trade poses a question: Who else will GM Mike Borgonzi look to trade before the deadline? We’ve identified three players Borgonzi should keep as opposed to trading away. RB Tony Pollard Tony Pollard is the player most linked to a trade following the Simmons departure. It’s easy to understand why. Pollard has been excellent in recent weeks, rushing for five touchdowns across the previous two contests, with back-to-back 100+ rushing yard performances. The former Memphis standout is on an expiring contract, but perhaps the Titans should consider re-signing him if his current form keeps up. DE Jacob Martin Jacob Martin is almost certain to draw trade interest around the league. Following his 3-sack performance versus the Cincinnati Bengals, the underrated veteran is now tied for fifth in sacks (6.5) in the entire league. Martin knows this Robert Saleh defense inside-out, and he’s signed through next campaign (2027), with a reasonable cap charge of $5.5 million. He’s outperforming his contract at a team-friendly number. CB Alontae Taylor The Alontae Taylor situation is unfortunate. The Titans clearly miscalculated his ability to play boundary cornerback when they signed him to a three-year, $58 million contract. They’ve reversed course and made him the league’s most expensive nickelback. He was also the backup nickel in Weeks 6-8 until Marcus Harris got injured versus the Bengals. The Titans probably won’t be able to trade him. They need to continue working on the best in-house solution.

title: Washington Commanders vs LA Rams Week 9: Five Questions with Turf Show Times
summary: It’s week 9 of the NFL season and the 2-4-1 Washington Commanders will be facing a 4-4 Rams team at home at Northwest Stadium on Sunday at 1:00 p.m. ET. The Rams started the season hyped as the best team in the NFL and presented as likely Super Bowl winners, but have struggled with consistency […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CA -DECEMBER 17: Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford (9) stands in the pocket to deliver a pass during third quarter action against the Washington Commanders at SoFi Stadium on December 17, 2023. (Photo by Jonathan Newton/The Washington Post via Getty Images) It’s week 9 of the NFL season and the 2-4-1 Washington Commanders will be facing a 4-4 Rams team at home at Northwest Stadium on Sunday at 1:00 p.m. ET. The Rams started the season hyped as the best team in the NFL and presented as likely Super Bowl winners, but have struggled with consistency since then. At the same time, the Rams are a talented and well-coached team, having blown out the Giants 28-6 in Week 2 and the Chargers 24-9 last week. On offense, the Rams are coached by head coach Sean McVay, offensive coordinator Nate Scheelhaase, and assistant HC Kliff Kingsbury, with McVay calling the plays. Two of those three coaches should be familiar to Washington fans as they were former playcallers here. This offense is built around one of the NFL’s best offensive lines , a gap-scheme run game that favors power, and the NFL’s highest use of 3-TE sets . It’s an offense that sets up to bludgeon opposing defenses in the run game, but also uses their heavy personnel tendency to force opposing defenses to go heavy and set up star WR Puka Nacua to feast on heavier, slower defensive matchups. This kind of offense funnels the ball to Nacua, who currently leads the NFL with a 37.9% target share . A ruptured hamstring by WR Davante Adams will only increase the likelihood of the Rams going heavy and throwing the ball to Nacua. Overall, the Rams have the 3rd-ranked passing offense and the 6th-ranked rushing offense in terms of yards per game. On defense, the Rams have been led by DC Chris Shula, who has worked his way up from being the assistant linebackers coach of the Rams in 2017. Shula has typically employed a 3-4 front with heavy use of zone coverage on the backend, though he is also known for extensive use of disguise, both on his pressure packages (faking a blitz from one direction while actually bringing pressure from another), and in his coverage (rotating coverages post-snap to confuse QBs). This year, after the Rams traded a 1st-round pick for shutdown CB Trent McDuffie, they have occasionally been using him to shadow star WRs, which allowed him to erase Malik Nabers in their Week 2 matchup. However, McDuffie’s status is uncertain this week after sustaining a back injury against the Chargers. The Rams also just lost star CB Jaylen Watson to a season-ending shoulder injury, which could leave the backend of the Rams defense weakened. At the same time, Los Angeles may be getting back star pass rusher Myles Garrett this week, which would be a tremendous boon for their defense. Overall, the Rams have run one of the NFL’s best defenses this year by many metrics, though it has ranked better against the pass (7th) than run (15th) . I asked Kenneth Arthur of Turf Show Times five questions to better understand the state of the Rams and what to look for in this game. 1) The Rams entered the season widely considered an elite team and Super Bowl favorite, but sit at 4-4 and on the outside looking in to win their division. Why has their season started off much slower than expected? I’d start with revisiting why the Rams were considered such heavy favorites. A perennial contender under Sean McVay, the reigning MVP, then they add Myles Garrett, Trent McDuffie, and Aaron Donald, right? Garrett hasn’t played since Week 1. McDuffie has missed a couple of games. Donald isn’t more than a rotational option at this point in his career. But that doesn’t explain everything, right? Well, the Rams are the perfect example of an “Achilles” or a “Goliath”. They look dangerous but they always have the same weak points. I wasn’t convinced the Rams were Super Bowl favorites going into the season because they didn’t fix special teams, they didn’t use the draft to make their team better now, and they have too many players who are on the precipice of another injury, such as Puka Nacua, Davante Adams, and Matthew Stafford. Nacua has been banged up, Adams is out 6-10 weeks, and Stafford is dealing with elbow soreness. Jaylen Watson, another big free agent addition, has also been banged up and aggravated a shoulder injury on Sunday. Special teams is awful, the receiver corps is thin, and the defense has predictable holes at linebacker. The defensive line was further weakened with injuries to Kobie Turner and Poona Ford. Overall, it’s a banged up team with bad special teams and they were very close to wins over the Broncos and Bills anyway. I think the bigger concern is losing to the Cardinals. However, Garrett is returning to practice this week, so it’s possible we see the closest thing to the version of the Rams people thought they’d be when those predictions were made. 2) The Rams have had a disastrous performance on special teams so far this year. What are some of the specific problems the Rams special teams have faced, how are they dealing with them, and what do you think they will be like going forward? The Rams have had bad special teams almost since McVay took over. He fired popular coordinator John Fassell a few years into the job and it’s been downhill since then. L.A. won’t focus any effort on finding a reliable kicker. They had Matt Gay and then let him walk in free agency over money. Now they’re on their third kicker–but last week they had TWO active kickers, so they’re almost on their fourth. Not locking down a good kicker is a big reason that the magnifying glass is on L.A.’s special teams. Kickoff coverage has always been weak and the Rams don’t even really try to understand the new rules. They are 27th in kickoff yard average and 32nd in punts that land inside the 20. Punter Ethan Evans has a big leg but won’t be known for technique or accuracy, nor does he have good coverage. Special teams coordinator Bubba Ventrone (fired by the Broncos last season) is just the latest in a long line of people to have that job. He probably won’t last long either. The Rams have signed a few special teamers during the year in an effort to improve, like Grant Stuard and Alex Bachman, but it’s not much and not having an impact. They will continue to be bad moving forward. That’s what I predict. 3) The Rams have been really efficient in the draft, with late-round gems like Puka Nacua, but at the same time have seemed to devalue high draft picks and preferred to trade them away for known NFL quantities. What do you think of this approach of GM Les Snead in recent years with respect to draft picks and roster construction? I would disagree that the Rams have been “efficient”, or even successful, in the draft. I think Puka Nacua is doing all the heavy lifting in that argument, but I’ll give two more: Kyren Williams in the 5th and Quentin Lake in the 6th in 2022. L.A. drafted three starting quality players on day two in 2023 (Byron Young, Steve Avila, Turner), and then RT Warren McClendon and Nacua on day three, and a couple of role players. That’s all fine. The biggest issues start in 2024, which is why the Rams are so thin at certain positions now. First-round pick Jared Verse was very overrated and that’s proving out in Cleveland. Second-round pick Braden Fiske (the Rams traded a future second-round pick to move up for Fiske, one of the biggest day two overpays in history) has regressed. Third-round picks Blake Corum and Kam Kinchens are “OK”. Then the Rams made six day three picks and none of them are consequential players, if they’re even still on the team. The 2025 draft saw the Rams pick six players, with second-round pick TE Terrance Ferguson on IR and yet to contribute much. Third-round OLB Josaiah Stewart contributes here and there, but we’ll see how much higher his ceiling is. Four day three picks aren’t contributing and two of them are off the team. Then the Rams drafted five players in 2026 and none of them…

full_text: The Commanders need reinforcements along the defensive line, like, in the worst possible way. Daron Payne is done for the season. Javon Kinlaw’s also on injured reserve. That’s why the fact that Johnny Newton practiced in full for a second straight day matters so much. He’s working to come off injured reserve, with his 21-day practice window having been opened up last week. There’s no guarantee that he’ll return in time for Sunday afternoon’s game against the Los Angeles Rams, but the odds seem better with him working so much in practice. He’s returning from a pectoral injury suffered during the preseason. Treylon Burks missed a second straight day with a foot injury, a bad sign considering how much and how well he played against the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 8. Stefon Diggs was back to work after receiving some veteran rest and, overall, the injury report is pretty light compared to recent weeks. John Bates, Sam Cosmi and Shy Tuttle were limited for a second straight day. Receiver Dyami Brown was a new addition to the participation report as limited with a calf injury, which generally implies that he got injured during Wednesday’s practice. title: Daronte Jones and David Blough talk injuries, Puka Nacua, and the visiting Rams
summary: The second day of practice means Washington Commanders coordinators Daronte Jones and David Blough are up at the podium for their weekly media sessions. They both got their second career wins at this level when the Commanders beat the Eagles 27-10 last week. The Rams are coming to town for the Commanders second straight home […]
full_text: The second day of practice means Washington Commanders coordinators Daronte Jones and David Blough are up at the podium for their weekly media sessions. They both got their second career wins at this level when the Commanders beat the Eagles 27-10 last week. The Rams are coming to town for the Commanders second straight home game, and they bring a new set of challenges with starters like Myles Garrett, Aaron Donald, Matthew Stafford, and Puka Nacua demanding attention whenever they’re on the field. Daronte Jones’ defense looked improved over the Tanner McKee-led Eagles, but the Rams aren’t tanking, and the Commanders will need all hands on deck on Sunday if the team wants to stay alive in the NFC East’s sad division race. Puka Nacua and Matthew Stafford will have opportunities to make plays. Jones was asked about having DBs trail receivers, but said Nacua can put them in “a space they’re not used to” and quick passes to allow him to “become more of a running back” after catching the ball. David Blough talked about coaching against his former teammate Matt Stafford, and former coaching mentor Kliff Kingsbury. He still talks with Kingsbury, who has called him in support after some low moments this season. Kingsbury and the Commanders “mutually agreed to part ways” earlier this year after he had served as the offensive coordinator for the prior two seasons. Aaron Donald returned from retirement this year, and Blough was asked about double-teaming him. “They don’t just allow you to double team Aaron Donald,” and mentioned other defensive linemen like Byron Young and the returning Myles Garrett. title: Commanders – Nick Cross: greatest defensive alignment diversity in NFL
summary: The Daily Slop – 5 November 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Sports Illustrated Commanders’ […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CA - OCTOBER 19: Nick Cross #25 of the Washington Commanders exits the field during an NFL football game against the San Francisco 49ers at Levi's Stadium on October 19, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Daily Slop – 5 November 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links a night to remember pic.twitter.com/WjJnkEooj7 — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) November 4, 2026 Articles Sports Illustrated Commanders’ Unique Usage of Safety Nick Cross Could Have Long-Term Implications Nick Cross’ expanded slot role gives Washington more options and could influence Mike Sainristil’s playing time and how the secondary is built Washington Commanders safety Nick Cross has greater alignment diversity than any NFL defender, according to SumerSports data through Week 8. The interesting part is that Cross’ position designation captures only part of what defensive coordinator Daronte Jones asks him to do. So, then the real question becomes: What does Washington gain by moving him around this much? Cross gives Jones a 212-pound safety who can play closer to the run game and be used as a blitzer. He can also move back to a deeper alignment on the next snap. Washington doesn’t have to take him off the field to change his job. Cross earned his two highest overall PFF grades of the season against San Francisco and Philadelphia. The Eagles game was also his strongest in run defense and tackling, backing up what Quinn saw near the line. Moving Cross around only helps if the other ten defenders are on the same page. Cross’ work at nickel also gives Jones an alternative to Mike Sainristil , who didn’t play a defensive snap against Philadelphia. Cross still has something to prove in coverage. PFF has charged him with 10 receptions on 11 targets for 69 yards and one touchdown across four appearances, with a 56.2 coverage grade. Those catches averaged 6.9 yards, so opponents haven’t piled up yardage in that sample. The figures include all his coverage work, not just his plays from the slot. If Cross proves he can cover consistently from the slot, Washington could have less need for a dedicated nickel corner. That would give general manager Adam Peters more flexibility to prioritize outside corners or depth elsewhere in the secondary. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Safety separation prevented & on ball grade through week 8 pic.twitter.com/QcEMh58get — Jrfortgang (@throwthedamball) November 4, 2026 There is no defender in the league who has more alignment diversity than Nick Cross. Daronte Jones has him lined up all over the formation for the Commanders (Data from @SumerSports ) pic.twitter.com/JHgTvkubeU — Tej Seth (@tejfbanalytics) November 4, 2026 Good third-down pressure to get Washington's defense off the field. 7-man pressure front vs. 6 blockers. Philly adjusts for the DBL-A mug and Sonny Styles, while Washington bluffs Sonny and drops Dorance Armstrong. Nice fire zone, creating a free rush for Nick Cross. pic.twitter.com/HlvLQrvai3 — Jamual (@LetMualTellit) November 4, 2026 The Athletic (paywall) How should the Commanders approach the trade deadline? Here are some options Should the Commanders buy, sell or stand pat? Jhabvala: Stand pat. Payne was their best option in a trade, but any deal is off the table because of his injury . The team doesn’t have many other obvious candidates who have the contract, position and potential value to be enticing to other teams. Two who could be of interest are safety Nick Cross and edge rusher Dorance Armstrong (No. 46 on The Athletic ’s big board ). Cross is only 25, has the versatility to play as many snaps at free safety as he does in the box, would have a minimal cap hit for an acquiring team and is particularly good as a run-stopper and blitzer. But to get rid of your top safety and a leader of the secondary when the playoffs are technically still in play wouldn’t seem to make much sense. It’s not like the Commanders have much depth on the back end. Armstrong, 29, has taken on more of a reserve role in Daronte Jones’ defense, but is still effective as a pass rusher (he’s averaging the fourth-most pressures per game for Washington at 2.17). He’s also on an expiring contract. Aldridge: It’s a recurring theme with this year’s team, but they’re kind of stuck. With Payne’s injury, I don’t really see an obvious trade candidate among the team’s young veterans (and, obviously, Washington won’t likely trade any of the high-profile free agents it just signed, like Cross, Odafe Oweh or Amik Robertson, who would bring back decent to good pick value in return). The Rams are playing better, but they’re still really banged up, so I’d be surprised if Washington isn’t at least in Sunday’s game. And if they were to beat Los Angeles … I mean, how could you then turn around and punt (no pun intended) on the rest of this season by moving guys at the deadline? To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Bullock’s Film Room (subscription) Commanders Film Review: Pass Rush vs Eagles Coming off the bye, they were hoping to turn things around and against the Eagles they certainly did. They delivered five sacks and multiple other pressures. According to NextGenStats, the Commanders had a season-high pressure rate at 46.5%. When they blitzed, they had a pressure rate of 83.3%, the second highest pressure rate on blitzes by any team in the NFL this season. So how did the Commanders do it? During the bye week, I wrote about some schemes that worked which they could use more frequently, and we definitely saw them come up against the Eagles on Sunday night. Things like read blitzes, disguised overloads and B gap stabs were all effective against the Eagles. The Commanders pass rush was under the microscope over the bye week, but against the Eagles they generated 5 sacks and a ton of pressure. Is this sustainable success? I took a closer look: https://t.co/7k6fTzlSnl pic.twitter.com/5QKuOo7s0u — Mark Bullock (@MarkBullockNFL) November 4, 2026 On this play, Oweh takes quite a wide alignment prior to the snap, but at the snap he works almost directly up the field. Mailata fans out towards him, cutting off his speed rush, but Oweh hits him with a nice cross chop move. Oweh reaches across Mailata’s body with his inside hand, chopping down with it as he makes contact with Mailata’s outside hand. Oweh then backs that up with his own outside hand chopping down to ensure Mailata’s outside hand is out of action. As a result, Oweh clears himself a path to the edge. He bends around the edge and rips through with his inside arm to break free of Mailata and close on the quarterback for the Commanders fifth sack of the game. Overall, the Commanders will of course be happy with the uptick from their pass rush unit in this game. They generated much more consistent pressure and of course finished those plays, putting up five sacks. However, this felt to me much more like the Eagles offensive line being bad than the Commanders pass rush being exceptionally good. Don’t get me wrong, you can only play against whoever the opponent puts out there each week, so I’m not trying to discredit this performance. But I do wonder how sustainable it is. The Commanders blitzed at a significantly lower rate than they have done all season. Much of these pressures and sacks came on four-man rushes. We’ve seen through the first six games of the season that this pass rush isn’t good enough to consistently win with four, and that Daronte Jones has had to blitz a lot and dial up various pressure packages in order to generate consistent pressure. This game doesn’t line up with that theme so far this season, which speaks to an issue with the Eagles offensive line rather than some big adjustment the Commanders made over…
