title: What has gone right -- and wrong -- for 10 new NFL head coaches in 2026 season
summary: There are 10 new head coaches in the NFL this season, which ties the most ever. How are things going for each of them after eight weeks?
full_text:
The  2026 NFL offseason featured 10 head coaching changes, which tied with 1978, 1997, 2006 and 2022 for the most ever in an offseason, per ESPN Research.

 The Raiders hired Klint Kubiak after his Super Bowl win  as the Seahawks' offensive coordinator. Three AFC North teams -- the Browns (Todd Monken), Steelers (Mike McCarthy) and Ravens (Jesse Minter) -- also changed coaches. Elsewhere in the AFC, the Bills promoted offensive coordinator Joe Brady to head coach, the Dolphins hired former Packers DC Jeff Hafley, and the Titans brought in Robert Saleh. In the NFC, Mike LaFleur, Kevin Stefanski and John Harbaugh were hired by the Cardinals, Falcons and Giants, respectively.

 How have these new coaches fared at their new destinations? We called on our NFL Nation reporters to evaluate both the positive and concerning signs from each team so far. Then, we provided a key stat on each team's start.

 The 10 teams with new coaches are listed below by ESPN Football Power Index 's playoff odds. We'll start in Western New York.

 

 
 Jump to a team: 
 ARI | ATL | BAL  |  BUF | CLE 
 LV | MIA  |  NYG | PIT | TEN 

 
 

 

 Joe Brady, Buffalo Bills 
 Record: 6-1 
 FPI chance to make playoffs:  99.4%

 What has gone right this season:  Brady's offense, and his partnership with quarterback  Josh Allen , is working. The Bills lead the NFL in points per game (33.3) and rank second in both yards per game and yards per play. The  trade for wide receiver  DJ Moore in the spring has made the Bills' offense more vertical, with Allen leading the NFL in yards per pass attempt (8.7). And their red zone rushing attack, led by Allen and RB  James Cook III , has them converting red zone trips into touchdowns at a 70% clip.

 What has gone wrong this season:  The pass defense has been a mess. The Bills have already moved on from safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson and benched cornerback Maxwell Hairston . Nickelback  Dee Alford has been in and out of the lineup with injuries . Now, the Bills are relying on a rookie and a couple of players who started the season on the practice squad to take significant snaps for a unit that ranks 30th in yards allowed per game. -- Nick Suss, Bills reporter 

 Key stat to know:  This is the second time in the past 30 seasons that Buffalo has started 6-1 or better. The last such start was in 2022, when it finished 13-3 and lost to the Bengals in the divisional round of the playoffs.  -- ESPN Research 

 

 
 

 Mike McCarthy, Pittsburgh Steelers 
 Record: 6-2 
 FPI chance to make playoffs:  81.0%

 What has gone right this season:  A Pittsburgh native, McCarthy took the job with a special understanding of the core identity of the team. Halfway through his first season, he has upheld that in a big way. Led by running back Jaylen Warren and a young core of offensive linemen, the Steelers' offense is a physical unit capable of creating explosive plays in the run game. Defensively, McCarthy brought in coordinator Patrick Graham to reinforce those classic principles with his 3-4 front. The Steelers have held opponents to a league-best 51.3 rushing yards per game in the past three games.

 

 What has gone wrong this season:  While McCarthy was brought in to maximize quarterback Aaron Rodgers , the passing game still lacks consistency. The Steelers rank 20th in passing yards per game (210.5) and 21st in air yards per attempt (6.5). And it's not all on Rodgers. Top receiver DK Metcalf has been plagued by drops, including one this past Sunday that resulted in an interception. The strong run game has carried the offense in the open field, but the Steelers are scoring touchdowns on only 50% of their red zone trips (tied for 26th in the NFL). Part of the problem is the playcalling. In the past four games, the Steelers utilized designed runs on just 31% of plays in goal-to-go situations. -- Brooke Pryor, Steelers reporter 

 Key stat to know:  The Steelers have a 4-0 record at home in 2026, which is their first such start since going 6-0 at home in 2020. And McCarthy's offense has shown up at Acrisure Stadium, averaging 27.8 points per game there versus 17.3 on the road. -- ESPN Research 

 

 
 

 John Harbaugh, New York Giants 
 Record: 4-2-1 
 FPI chance to make playoffs:  47.0%

 What has gone right this season:  A lot. The Giants have already matched their win total from 2025. They're clearly a more buttoned-up and fundamentally sound team after repping situational football endlessly in training camp. And they're 3-1-1 in one-score games after finishing 1-7 last season. The biggest gains have been made by their special teams (ranked eighth in EPA) and defense (ninth overall). Hiring defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson has worked out, as Wilson has done a solid job with a group that isn't loaded with talent and lost its best player in edge rusher  Brian Burns  ( torn ACL ). They're allowing 46.5 fewer yards per game than last season.

 What has gone wrong this season:  Injuries have hit the Giants hard. They lost Burns and starting quarterback Jaxson Dart  ( left knee injury ), arguably the two most important players on each side of the ball, for the season. New York spent the spring and summer creating an offense that prioritizes the quarterback's legs and had to pivot. Offensive coordinator Matt Nagy has made it work relatively well with Dart, Jameis Winston and now J.J. McCarthy . But the injuries still have the Giants working with limitations. Their quarterbacks are averaging 13.2 yards rushing per game since Dart's injury.  -- Jordan Raanan, Giants reporter 

 Key stat to know: After their Week 7 win  over the Texans, the Giants became the favorites to win the NFC East (-150 on DraftKings), the first time since 2016 that has happened at any point during a season. That year, they finished 11-5 and lost in the wild-card round  to the Packers.

 

 
 

 Todd Monken, Cleveland Browns 
 Record: 5-3 
 FPI chance to make playoffs:  16.8%

 What has gone right this season:  The Browns are the second-youngest team in the NFL but have taken on a gritty, resilient persona behind Monken to help them dominate late-game situations. All five of Cleveland's wins have been courtesy of game-winning drives. "Coach Monk has put us in these situations in practice time after time ... so whenever we get into the game and whenever we get into these situations, we already have the confidence to go down there and set up a game-winning drive," rookie wide receiver KC Concepcion said.

 

 What has gone wrong this season:  The offense -- Monken's area of expertise -- remains a work in progress. Quarterback Deshaun Watson has raised his level of play this season but still ranks 28th out of 30 qualifying players in QBR, and he could miss Week 9 after being put in concussion protocol . Inconsistent play from a new-look offensive line has also contributed to an offense that ranks 29th in points per game (17.4). "It's been a little bit of an up-and-down challenge," Monken said. "But that's part of the NFL, right? That's part of when you play the best in the world as you're trying to find your way, your footing, your players, coaches, schematically, to be consistent." -- Daniel Oyefusi, Browns reporter 

 Key stat to know: Monken's team has already surpassed the Browns' win total from 2024 (three) and is one win away from beating Cleveland's 2025 total. Before Sunday's loss to the Steelers, Cleveland's four straight wins in division games (dating back to last season) were its longest streak since 1987. -- ESPN Research 

 

 
 

 Klint Kubiak, Las Vegas Raiders 
 Record: 4-4 
 FPI chance to make playoffs:  10.7%

 What has gone right this season:  Despite the Raiders having an insufficient run game and weak WR room, they rank sixth in points per game (27.6) and 12th in total yards (342.4). That's because the dynamic between Kubiak and veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins has orchestrated one of the league's best passing games. Kubiak has been a good play designer, while Cousins' knowledge…

title: What turned around Washington's defense?
summary: Safety NIck Cross and LB Dorance Armstrong missed time but are beginning to jell with the new pass rushers.
full_text:
ASHBURN, Va. -- Midway through the first quarter Sunday, the Washington Commanders ' offseason vision for its pass rush came to light. They showed seven defenders at the line of scrimmage; both inside linebackers stood at the line on either side of the center.

 Then came the organized chaos and, for Washington, the fun. And a blueprint for what the Commanders (2-4-1) need to compensate for losing its top two defensive linemen, if it wants to turn its season around -- starting Sunday vs. the Rams (4-4).

 After all, they spent nearly $100 million in guaranteed money in the offseason to help the pass rush. It needs to help lead any resurgence and that was the case in Week 8.

 "It was definitely a snapshot of what we can be," Washington defensive coordinator Daronte Jones said. "Now it's just about consistency."

 If they find it, it would provide a big boost -- especially with linemen Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw both out for the season.

 "The better we are," outside linebacker Dorance Armstrong said of the pass rush, "the better our defense is. Everyone knows that."

 Numerous plays showed their ability to pressure the passer. But this third-down play vs. the Eagles in Week 8 showed what can happen when they work more together, as Jones and coach Dan Quinn have wanted.

 At the snap on this third-and-6, inside linebacker Sonny Styles dropped into coverage as did Armstrong. The edge rusher on the right side,  K'Lavon Chaisson , stepped forward, drew the attention of the left tackle, then looped inside with tackle Charles Omenihu moving outside.

 That's all safety Nick Cross needed for a free rush off the edge, and that forced Eagles quarterback Tanner McKee to throw a deep out early and the pass fell 5 yards from its intended target.

 It was coordinated. It was effective. It didn't result in a huge play, but it incorporated what they had hoped. And it wasn't the only time this happened in that 27-10 win; they pressured McKee on a season-high 46.5% of dropbacks.

 "Last week gives you a snapshot of when guy are working in unison, whether it's a four-man or five-man [rush]," Jones said, "you never know who's going to make the play or who may come to life. As long as we're doing those things consistently there's some shining light to be seen."

 The trick will be incorporating this level of pressure vs. the Rams' Matthew Stafford , one of the hardest quarterbacks to harass. He ranks fourth in terms of pressure rate and eighth in the league in quickest release. He's also thrown 80 play-action passes, another way to try to slow the pass rush.

 "It's all about the rush in the middle of the pocket," Chaisson said. "It's about getting hands in the face, making him uncomfortable, making it muddy and getting the offensive linemen to step on his toes, hit him on his follow through, anything you can do to disrupt the timing and rhythm."

 

 Finally, teams pressure him on only 37.6% of their blitzes -- the fourth-lowest rate in the league.

 "There's obviously a philosophy that allows the blitz to sometimes not be as successful," Jones said, "because of the way Matthew Stafford sees the game."

 But the Commanders' hope is that the pass rush will continue to impact opposing quarterbacks. They spent $99.5 million in guaranteed money on players who can affect the passer, from outside linebackers Odafe Oweh ($68 million) and Chaisson ($10.3 million) to Cross ($4 million). They drafted Styles with the seventh overall pickto help in coverage but also as a blitzer.

 "We've always known what we had," defensive lineman Deatrich Wise Jr . said. "We are putting the pieces together for four quarters straight."

 Too often early in the season the rush wasn't as coordinated, Oweh said in September. It would lead to gaps in the rush, allowing quarterbacks to escape. Some of that stemmed from playing in a new system under Jones; some of that was due to having four new starters in their front seven.

 "They were more coordinated and connected than we have been," Quinn said. "That's the steps I'm looking to see."

 It took time in part because Oweh and Chaisson missed nearly a month of practice in training camp with soft-tissue injuries.

 Their top pass rusher from 2025, Armstrong, tore his ACL in Week 7 and though he returned to practice on Aug. 7 he was slowly worked back into the lineup - and the NFL suspended him for Week 1 because of their personal conduct policy.

 Armstrong said he's just now feeling like he was prior to the knee injury when he had 5.5 sacks and seven tackles for a loss in six full games. Sunday, he recorded his first sack and first tackle for a loss.

 "Just getting back to what I'm used to doing," Armstrong said.

 He provides a different look than Chaisson and Oweh, using more power -- which also enables him to rush inside in some packages. Oweh leads Washington with four sacks; Chaisson has 3.5 -- he also has a team-best 22 pressures and 11 quarterback hits.

 "We're just trusting what the coaches are telling us," Oweh said. "We know the sacks are going to come with reps and everyone trusting each other as pass rushers, and it showed last weekend."

 The last piece that made a difference Sunday -- and, the Commanders hope it does so over the next 10 games, was the return of corner Trey Amos and Cross. Amos was Washington's best corner as a rookie last season until fracturing his leg in Week 10. He then practiced just once in camp before suffering an ankle injury that kept him out until Week 6.

 Cross suffered an internal injury in Week 2 that required surgery and also kept him out until Week 6. He's key to the secondary because of his versatility: he lines up at linebacker, in the slot, at free and strong safety.

 But he's also their best blitzer from the secondary. He's blitzed 15 times in four games; the other nine defensive backs have combined for 31. Jones said Cross' presence allows them to use different packages, allowing for more versatility.

 "Nick is a gem," Oweh said. "He's a great defensive player. He does it all, very cerebral guy. It's always good to have him there."

 All of it adds up why the Commanders like where the defense is headed -- provided the pass rush becomes consistent.

 "The sky's the limit," Armstrong said. "Everybody knows what we're all capable of but we're just now getting to have the opportunity to play together. As long as we keep getting better with that each week we should produce more."
